item.title: Oakland: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Oakland housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $710,647, up 0.56 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Oakland's chain of title starts with one land grant. In 1820 the last Spanish governor of California gave Sergeant Luis Maria Peralta about 44,800 acres covering what is now Oakland, Berkeley, Alameda, Emeryville, Piedmont and San Leandro. The United States took California, the Land Act of 1851 made the family prove the grant in court, and by the time the Supreme Court confirmed it in 1856 squatters held most of it. Six acres survived as a park.

Then the city ate its neighbours. In 1897 it annexed Temescal, Golden Gate, Bushrod and the Piedmont Avenue area. In 1909 it took Fruitvale, Elmhurst, Melrose and Fitchburg in the largest annexation it ever made, carrying the city from 22.9 square miles to roughly 60 while the population doubled to 150,174 by 1910, most of that from people who left San Francisco after the 1906 earthquake.

A few things here are genuinely first in the country. The state legislature protected Lake Merritt in 1870, making it the first wildlife refuge in North America. Frederick Law Olmsted, who designed Central Park, laid out Mountain View Cemetery in 1863. The 16th Street Station opened in 1912 as the western terminus of the transcontinental railroad and became the western headquarters of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters.

The hills tell a different story. The San Antonio redwood forest was big enough that ships entering San Francisco Bay steered by two of its trees to clear Blossom Rock, and it was logged level inside about fifteen years. On October 20, 1991 the Tunnel Fire killed 25 people and destroyed 2,843 single family homes across those same hills.

What all of that produces is a city of 191,713 housing units where 46.6 percent predate 1950. Twenty miles south in Fremont that figure is 2 percent. Only 41.5 percent of Oakland units are single family detached and owner occupancy is 42.3 percent, so this is substantially a flats and multi unit market. Zillow tracks 121 separate neighborhoods inside the city.

So Oakland is not one market, it is three. Pre war flats, where the questions are the legal unit count, the rent rules and a long inspection list. The hills, where fire insurance decides affordability before the house does. And downtown, where it is reserve studies and seismic retrofit.

Find out which one you are shopping in before you compare a single price, and pull the year built before anything else.

What the market is doing right now

The value index puts a typical Oakland home at $710,647 on 2026-09-30, up 0.56 percent month over month and up 0.6 percent year over year.

Listing activity in Oakland for 2026-09. Active inventory is 527, up 7.1 percent from the prior month and down 29.2 percent from a year earlier. 316 new listings came on, up 25.0 percent month over month, and 228 went pending. Median days on market is 40, down 1.1 percent month over month and down 9.4 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $674,250 at $494 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,394 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,706.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $710,647, up 0.56 percent month over month, up 0.6 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $7,190, or $86,280 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.71 percent (Oakland effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 22 areas of Oakland. What each one actually is:

  • Acorn. Fifty blocks of this neighborhood were demolished.
  • Adams Point. Adams Point is named for Edson Adams, one of the men who got hold of Oakland's land early, and in 1906 it filled up with San Franciscans who had nowhere else to go.
  • Allendale. The Allendale tract map was recorded in 1892, and there was a cinema operating here by 1913.
  • Brookfield Village. Twelve hundred houses went up here during the Second World War and they sold for four thousand dollars each.
  • Bushrod. Bushrod was annexed by Oakland in 1897, in the same batch as Temescal, Golden Gate and Piedmont Avenue, and that date is the most solid thing in its published record.
  • Caballo Hills. Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Castlemont. Castlemont takes its name from the high school at its centre, and its published history is thin enough that this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Chabot Park. Anthony Chabot dammed a creek in 1868 and built Oakland its first water supply at municipal scale, and his name is on the parkland at the edge of this neighborhood.
  • Chinatown. Oakland Chinatown is older than almost everything around it.
  • Clawson. Clawson is the official name, and a good number of people call this ground Dogtown.
  • Cleveland Heights. Cleveland Heights is the slope on the east side of Lake Merritt, and the hook here is the ground itself: it climbs, so the houses look back across the water at downtown.
  • Clinton San Antonio. Clinton and San Antonio sit east of Lake Merritt on ground that was two separate towns before Oakland absorbed them, and the street grid still shows the seam.
  • Columbia Gardens. Columbia Gardens is one of three neighborhoods in the deepest part of East Oakland, with Brookfield Village and Sobrante Park, and one local account calls the three of them independent but intertwined.
  • Crestmont. Crestmont is a hillside pocket on the Oakland ridge with little published history of its own, so this is the development record and the practical read.
  • Dimond. Hugh Dimond came over for the Gold Rush, made money in the Mariposa and Tuolumne mines, and in 1867 bought 267 acres of Oakland foothill along Sausal Creek.
  • Dogtown. Dogtown is a nickname, and the official name of this ground is Clawson.
  • Downtown. Downtown Oakland's commercial centre was fixed at Ninth Street and Broadway by 1877, and Broadway has been the spine ever since.
  • Eastlake. Eastlake is the commercial and residential district immediately east of Lake Merritt, and like several of the older Oakland flats it has very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Eastmont. General Motors built cars here for about fifty years, then left, and the plant became a shopping mall, and the mall became a social services centre.
  • Elmhurst. Elmhurst was called Jones until 1869, and it was a train station before it was a town.
  • Fitchburg. Fitchburg was a town, Oakland annexed it in 1909, and the name has largely been replaced by Lockwood.
  • Glenview. The street you shop on in Glenview was a road for moving dead redwoods.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $7,190, $86,280 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Alameda County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $710,647 here, transfer tax runs about $11,441 at 16.10 dollars per thousand. Custom is to split it, so about $5,721 a side, and who pays is set by the contract.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. At $2,000,000 the rate steps from 16.10 to 18.60 per thousand, so a sale one dollar over that line pays about $5,000 more than a sale one dollar under it. On anything pricing near $2,000,000, the number to run is not the percentage. It is which side of the line the contract price lands on.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $10,660.

What waiting costs

The two year cost of waiting, price plus payment, comes to about $9,161 here. The five year figure is $27,880.

This rests on one observed year carried forward. The two year figure is the defensible one; the five year figure is arithmetic, not a forecast.

The full report

For the tables, the financing detail, the tax math, the holding costs, the buyer programs, the ADU rules and the sources, the full Oakland report has all of it. It is rebuilt every month when the new data publishes. Read it at https://myrealtoraye.github.io/neighborhood-reports/oakland/.

item.title: Berkeley: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Berkeley housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,442,475, up 0.90 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Berkeley's street grid is a railroad map. Shattuck Avenue, Adeline Street and Stanford Avenue all trace the Berkeley Branch line, completed in 1876, and Stanford Avenue carries the name of the railroad's president, Leland Stanford. Adeline's diagonal through South Berkeley is that old right of way, still there a century and a half later.

The city exists because of a land purchase and a merger. The private College of California bought the ground that is now the campus in 1866. On March 23, 1868, Governor Henry Haight signed the charter that merged it with the state's new college of agriculture and mechanical arts to create the University of California. It opened to forty students the next year and moved onto the Berkeley site in 1873. Sather Tower went up later, steel frame in 1914 and stone facade in 1915, paid for by Jane K. Sather in memory of her husband Peder and designed by John Galen Howard.

But the oldest part of town is nowhere near the campus. Captain James Jacobs built a freight wharf at the foot of what is now Delaware Street in 1853, William Bowen's inn opened on the stagecoach road in 1854, and the settlement between them was called Ocean View for the sight of the Pacific through the Golden Gate. Berkeley's first school opened there in 1856. When the city incorporated in 1878, Ocean View came in and was renamed West Berkeley.

Two days did more to shape the housing stock than any policy. On September 17, 1923 a fire out of Wildcat Canyon crossed the ridge and destroyed between 543 and 640 structures in the north hills, roughly 585 of them houses, putting about 4,000 people out of their homes with no deaths. The water mains in the burn area were two inches across. And the 1906 San Francisco earthquake sent a wave of buyers over the bay, breaking up the rural estates that became Elmwood.

Mason-McDuffie built much of the rest. The firm laid out Northbrae and Thousand Oaks, handed the city the land around five volcanic rock outcrops for parks in 1917, and also developed the modest San Pablo Park tract on the flats around Berkeley's oldest park, bought in 1907 for thirty five thousand dollars. Duncan McDuffie later ran the Sierra Club.

So Berkeley is four distinct markets: flats, hills, the campus perimeter and downtown. The inspection list, the insurance question and the zoning risk are different in each. Figure out which one you are shopping in before you compare a single price.

What the market is doing right now

Typical home value in Berkeley is $1,442,475 as of 2026-09-30, up 0.90 percent from the month before and up 8.0 percent over the year.

Listing activity in Berkeley for 2026-09. Active inventory is 97, up 4.2 percent from the prior month and down 1.2 percent from a year earlier. 92 new listings came on, up 54.2 percent month over month, and 45 went pending. Median days on market is 29, down 1.8 percent month over month and up 29.3 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $1,065,625 at $725 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,674 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,891.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,442,475, up 0.90 percent month over month, up 8.0 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $13,384, or $160,606 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 22 areas of Berkeley. What each one actually is:

  • Bateman. Nobody is entirely sure who Bateman was, and the neighborhood is named after him anyway.
  • Berkeley Hills. On September 17, 1923, a fire came over the ridge out of Wildcat Canyon and burned a large part of this area to the ground in a single afternoon.
  • Berkeley Marina. There is a pier here that used to run three and a half miles out into the bay.
  • Claremont. The Claremont Hotel could not legally serve a drink for decades, and the reason was a state law measured with a ruler.
  • Cragmont. Cragmont is named for the rock, and the rock is why the neighborhood looks the way it does.
  • Downtown Berkeley. Shattuck Avenue is wide and straight through downtown because it was a railroad before it was a street.
  • Elmwood. The oldest building in Elmwood's shopping district went up in 1907, one year after the San Francisco earthquake, and that timing explains how the neighborhood filled in.
  • Gilman District. Green Day's original graffiti is on a beam above the stage at 924 Gilman Street, from back when they were called Sweet Children.
  • Halcyon. Halcyon Court used to be a parking lot.
  • Le Conte. The neighborhood is still called Le Conte.
  • Lorin. Before Lorin was part of Berkeley it was its own settlement, and its train stop was a set of twelve wooden steps up to the tracks.
  • North Berkeley. North Berkeley's housing stock has a hard line running through it, and the line is a single day in 1923.
  • Northbrae. A real estate company gave this neighborhood its parks, and the rock the parks are built around has the neighborhood's name on it in the geology textbooks.
  • Ocean View. This is the oldest part of Berkeley.
  • Poets Corner. You can find this neighborhood on a map without being told where it is.
  • San Pablo Park. Berkeley bought the land for this park in 1907 for thirty five thousand dollars, and it is the oldest park the city owns.
  • South Berkeley. Adeline Street runs at an angle to everything around it, and the reason is a railroad built in 1876.
  • Southside. In May 1968 a group of activists turned a vacant lot at the southwest corner of Dwight Way and Telegraph Avenue into a park.
  • Thousand Oaks. Berkeley voters came 194 votes short of turning this entire neighborhood into a public park, and because they missed, you can buy a house here.
  • Uc Campus. Berkeley exists because a private college bought this land in 1866 and then handed itself over to the state.
  • West Berkeley. West Berkeley was a separate town called Ocean View, and it is older than the university.
  • Westbrae. Westbrae is named after a streetcar line, and the line's old roadbed is now the path you walk the dog on.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $13,384 a month, $160,606 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Alameda County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Figure $23,224 in transfer tax on a $1,442,475 sale here, at 16.10 dollars per thousand. Local practice splits it down the middle, roughly $11,612 each, though the contract decides.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. At $1,600,000 the rate steps from 16.10 to 26.10 per thousand, so a sale one dollar over that line pays about $16,000 more than a sale one dollar under it. On anything pricing near $1,600,000, the number to run is not the percentage. It is which side of the line the contract price lands on.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $21,637.

What waiting costs

Waiting two years at this place's own trailing rate costs about $278,021, counting the price increase and the payment increase together. Over five years it is $946,506.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

The full report

Everything behind these numbers lives in the full Berkeley report: the tables, the rate and loan detail, the tax math, holding costs, buyer programs, ADU rules and a dated source for each figure. It is rebuilt every month when the new data publishes. Read it at https://myrealtoraye.github.io/neighborhood-reports/berkeley/.

Written by Alex Bradeis. I publish one of these for every neighborhood I cover, every month, as the new numbers come out.

item.title: Albany: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Albany housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,237,577, up 0.59 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Albany is eight thousand homes between Berkeley and the county line, and nearly half of them are older than the Second World War.

Albany is a small city wedged between Berkeley and the Contra Costa line, and almost half of its housing is older than the Second World War. Solano Avenue is the commercial spine and it runs straight through into Berkeley. That is the practical fact about living here: the shopping street does not stop at the city line. Albany Hill rises at the western end, and the Albany waterfront and the Bulb sit beyond it on the bay.

Albany has 8,070 housing units and 48.7 percent of them predate 1950, one of the highest pre war shares in this series. 50.3 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 53.1 percent, the ACS median value is 1,202,200 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,445.

That pre war share is the organising fact. In a city this small, with stock this consistent in age, the inspection report is the whole negotiation.

So run the pre war list properly on anything you are serious about. Foundation bolting first, because it is both a structural and an insurance question. Then knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, the sewer lateral, the permit history on every addition, and the condition of original windows and siding.

Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, since conversions are common in housing this age and the paperwork often is not.

Check the lot dimensions and setbacks early if an accessory dwelling unit is part of your plan, because Albany lots are small and the setback, not the floor plan, is what decides it.

On Albany Hill and the slopes, add soils and drainage history, retaining structures and their ownership, and a written fire insurance quote on the exact address.

Then walk Solano Avenue from the address and keep walking into Berkeley. The fact that the commercial street does not stop at the city line is most of what the Albany premium buys, and you confirm it on foot.

What the market is doing right now

Typical home value in Albany is $1,237,577 as of 2026-09-30, up 0.59 percent from the month before and up 6.2 percent over the year.

Listing activity in Albany for 2026-09. Active inventory is 25, up 25.0 percent from the prior month and up 35.1 percent from a year earlier. 18 new listings came on, up 125.0 percent month over month, and 9 went pending. Median days on market is 25, down 54.2 percent month over month and up 41.4 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $669,000 at $602 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,170 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,685.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,237,577, up 0.59 percent month over month, up 6.2 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $11,602, or $139,219 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 4 areas of Albany. What each one actually is:

  • Albany Hill. Albany Hill is the rise at the western end of the city, and it is the one piece of Albany that is not flat.
  • San Pablo Avenue Corridor. San Pablo Avenue is Albany's other commercial street and it is a very different animal from Solano.
  • Solano Avenue District. Solano Avenue is the reason people move to Albany, and it does not stop at the city line.
  • The Circle. The Circle is the roundabout where Marin Avenue meets the hill, and the neighborhood around it takes the name.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $11,602, $139,219 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. In Alameda County the 2026 one-unit limit is $1,249,125. It serves as the conforming conventional ceiling and the FHA ceiling at once.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $1,237,577 here, transfer tax runs about $19,925 at 16.10 dollars per thousand. Custom is to split it, so about $9,962 a side, and who pays is set by the contract.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $18,564.

What waiting costs

On the same trailing rate, two years of waiting adds up to roughly $183,865 in price and payment combined, and five years to $609,356.

Treat it as a scenario, not a prediction. The appreciation input is one year of observed change carried forward, and five years of compounding on one year of data flatters the result.

The full report

The full Albany report carries the month over month tables, the loan and rate detail, the property tax math, the cost of holding, first-time buyer programs, ADU rules and the sources behind every figure. item.title: Emeryville: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Emeryville housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $429,369, up 0.03 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Emeryville incorporated to protect a racetrack.

Emeryville incorporated in December 1896, on the second by the city's own account and the eighth by another, and it did it to protect a racetrack. Temescal residents had proposed a town that would have covered this ground too. That alarmed the business owners here, and a large part of the push to form a separate town was keeping the California Jockey Club track and the gambling revenue that came with it. The place is named for Joseph Emery, who arrived in the Gold Rush and bought land here. The city also built a large park around its shellmound in the late 1800s. The boundaries drawn by the founders in 1896 are substantially the ones in force today.

What the city became after the track is an industrial town, and then, more recently, something close to a laboratory for dense housing. The figures are unlike anywhere else in this series.

Emeryville has 8,497 housing units and 12.1 percent of them predate 1950. Only 5.8 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 24.2 percent, both the lowest in this entire series. The ACS median value is 604,800 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,936. Hold those against Piedmont, eight minutes away, at 94.7 percent detached and 90.9 percent owner occupancy. Two cities in the same county could not be further apart in what they are built of.

So shopping Emeryville means shopping buildings, not houses.

Get the association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure. Ask what the association insures and what you insure. Ask whether the building has had a seismic retrofit and whether it is soft story, because a great deal of stock here sits over parking and lenders ask. Ask whether there has been construction defect litigation, and read the association minutes.

Pull the zoning for the parcel and everything touching it. This is a small city with industrial ground, active redevelopment and no spare land, so what is permitted next door frequently differs from what stands there, and a view is not a protected asset.

Then pull the actual tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

And on the bay side, get the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote and ask the inspector about settlement, because much of that ground is made land.

What the market is doing right now

As of 2026-09-30 the typical Emeryville home is worth $429,369. That is up 0.03 percent on the month and down 6.3 percent on the year.

Listing activity in Emeryville for 2026-09. Active inventory is 70, up 26.4 percent from the prior month and down 24.9 percent from a year earlier. 38 new listings came on, up 58.3 percent month over month, and 18 went pending. Median days on market is 36, down 25.3 percent month over month and down 29.6 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $585,194 at $530 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,020 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,945.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $429,369, up 0.03 percent month over month, down 6.3 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $4,572, or $54,860 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 6 areas of Emeryville. What each one actually is:

  • Bay Street. Bay Street is the retail centre of Emeryville and the housing built around it.
  • Doyle Hollis. Doyle and Hollis are the two streets this district is named for, in the middle of Emeryville.
  • East Baybridge. East BayBridge is the retail and housing development on Emeryville's southern edge, up against the Oakland line.
  • Park Avenue District. The Park Avenue District is the old industrial heart of Emeryville, and the brick buildings are the reason it looks different from everything around it.
  • The Triangle. The Triangle is the residential pocket of Emeryville, and it is the part of the city that looks most like a neighborhood instead of a development.
  • Watergate. Watergate is the tower complex on Emeryville's bay edge, and it is unlike anything else in this series.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $4,572 a month, $54,860 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. For 2026, one-unit financing in Alameda County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical Emeryville home, $429,369, comes to roughly $5,625 at a rate of 13.10 per thousand. It is normally split down the middle, about $2,812 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. At $1,000,000 the rate steps from 13.10 to 16.10 per thousand, so a sale one dollar over that line pays about $3,000 more than a sale one dollar under it. On anything pricing near $1,000,000, the number to run is not the percentage. It is which side of the line the contract price lands on.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $6,441.

What waiting costs

Hold off two years and the combined price and payment cost is near -$60,474. At five years it reaches -$166,249.

Treat it as a scenario, not a prediction. The appreciation input is one year of observed change carried forward, and five years of compounding on one year of data flatters the result.

The full report

The long version of this covers Emeryville in full, with the monthly tables, the financing detail, the property tax rules, cost of holding, programs, ADUs and every source dated. It is rebuilt every month when the new data publishes. Read it at https://myrealtoraye.github.io/neighborhood-reports/emeryville/.

item.title: Piedmont: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Piedmont housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $2,549,073, up 1.42 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Piedmont's boundaries were traced off a sewer map, in a hurry, to stop Oakland annexing it.

Piedmont exists because Oakland was about to swallow it. When it became clear that Oakland, wanting the tax base, was preparing to annex this hill, a charter was drawn up in a hurry and Piedmont incorporated on January 30, 1907. The boundaries were taken off a sewer line map, and that is why the city's edges weave in and out of Oakland the way they do. It became a charter city on December 18, 1922, and voters adopted the charter on February 27, 1923.

Piedmont has 4,073 housing units and 71.7 percent of them predate 1950, the highest pre war share of any city in this series. 94.7 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 90.9 percent, both also the highest. The ACS median value tops out at the Census ceiling of 2,000,001 dollars and the city ZHVI is 2,549,073.

Piedmont is also completely surrounded. Every road out of it runs into Oakland, and the neighborhoods on the other side of that line are Montclair, Grand Lake, Piedmont Avenue and Oakmore, each with its own market and its own rules. Mountain View Cemetery, laid out by Frederick Law Olmsted in 1863, sits just beyond the northern boundary.

Nothing else in these three counties looks like that. Emeryville, a few minutes away, runs 5.8 percent detached and 24.2 percent owner occupied. Piedmont is almost entirely century old houses owned by the people living in them.

So this is a single product market and the work is concentrated in two places.

The inspection, because the stock is old and large. Get a specialist inspection on anything pre 1930. Ask about foundation bolting first, then knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, the sewer lateral and the permit history on every addition. Ask whether any local historic designation applies before planning an exterior change. On the sloped parcels add soils and drainage history and the condition and ownership of any retaining structures.

And the boundary, because of how it was drawn. Piedmont's city line weaves in and out of Oakland block by block, and which side a parcel sits on decides the school district, the transfer tax and the services. Oakland charges 16.10 dollars per thousand in transfer tax at its typical value, and its brackets apply to the whole sale price instead of only the part above the line, so the difference between the two sides of that boundary is not a rounding error. Piedmont has 4,073 housing units in total, against Oakland's 191,713, and its city ZHVI of 2,549,073 dollars sits against Oakland's 710,647. Take the city from the assessor's parcel record, never from the mailing address, and run the transfer tax both ways before you model a net.

What the market is doing right now

As of 2026-09-30 the typical Piedmont home is worth $2,549,073. That is up 1.42 percent on the month and up 14.6 percent on the year.

Realtor.com does not publish monthly listing metrics for Piedmont, so there is no inventory, days on market or asking price figure to report here. The value series above is measured separately and is unaffected.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $2,549,073, up 1.42 percent month over month, up 14.6 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $23,009, or $276,110 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 3 areas of Piedmont. What each one actually is:

  • Central Piedmont. Central Piedmont is the civic middle of a city that exists because of a sewer map.
  • Lower Piedmont. Lower Piedmont is the edge where the city meets Oakland, and in places the boundary runs down the middle of a block.
  • Upper Piedmont. Upper Piedmont is the top of the hill, and it has the largest houses and the longest views in the city.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $23,009 a month, $276,110 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. For 2026, one-unit financing in Alameda County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

At 14.10 dollars per thousand, a $2,549,073 sale in Piedmont carries about $35,942 in transfer tax. It is normally split down the middle, about $17,971 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Emeryville at 26.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $63,727.

What waiting costs

Price and payment together, a two year wait here runs about $923,777. Stretch it to five and the figure is $3,474,044.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

item.title: Alameda: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Alameda housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,145,869, up 0.59 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Alameda has not been a peninsula since 1902. A tidal canal cut through the neck that connected it to Oakland, and the city has treated being an island as its governing fact ever since.

That shows up most clearly in the charter. In 1973 voters added Article 26 and banned new multifamily construction outright. In 1991 a second measure capped residential density citywide at one housing unit per 2,000 square feet of land. A repeal went to the voters in November 2020 as Measure Z and failed. State housing law has since created some room, and the clearest example is a project of roughly 1,200 units on the former naval air station. Anyone buying here should confirm the current rules with the city, because almost nothing about Alameda's housing supply makes sense without them.

The history behind the housing is unusually legible. Downtown exists because the San Francisco and Alameda Railroad stopped at what is now Lincoln and Park in 1864, and the National Register listed the Park Street Historic Commercial District in May 1982. The Gold Coast filled in with Victorians and Edwardians, with a second wave after the electric streetcar arrived in 1892. Neptune Beach ran at the west end from 1917 to 1939 and people called it the Coney Island of the West. Naval Air Station Alameda was commissioned on November 1, 1940, closed in April 1997, and left 1,560 acres that became a National Historic Landmark District in January 2013. South Shore and Bay Farm are younger than all of it because they were dredged out of the bay, starting when the dredge Franciscan arrived on November 7, 1955.

So Alameda is really three housing markets. Pre war stock on the original island, where the question is the condition of a hundred year old house. Mid century and later on engineered fill, where the question is settlement and flood insurance. And new construction at the Point, where the question is the environmental record and the assessments.

Figure out which of the three you are shopping in before you compare prices, because the right inspection, the right insurance question and the right risk are different in each one.

What the market is doing right now

Measured to 2026-09-30, typical value in Alameda is $1,145,869: up 0.59 percent against last month, up 2.1 percent against last year.

Listing activity in Alameda for 2026-09. Active inventory is 71, down 9.3 percent from the prior month and down 39.1 percent from a year earlier. 42 new listings came on, up 19.6 percent month over month, and 29 went pending. Median days on market is 34, down 2.7 percent month over month and up 14.1 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $972,000 at $617 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,573 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $4,181.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,145,869, up 0.59 percent month over month, up 2.1 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $10,804, or $129,647 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 14 areas of Alameda. What each one actually is:

  • Alameda Point. This is 1,560 acres of the island that belonged to the United States Navy until 1997, and the Secretary of the Interior made the heart of it a National Historic Landmark District in January 2013.
  • Ballena Bay. Ballena Bay is an island off the side of an island, and a good part of it runs on a lease from the city.
  • Bay Farm. A man named Amos Mecartney tried to farm this ground in the 1870s and it did not work out.
  • Bronze Coast. The Bronze Coast sits between the Gold Coast and the rest of the island, and the name tells you exactly what it is: the same era, a step down in scale.
  • Central Alameda. Central Alameda is the part of the island everybody drives through and nobody can draw the boundary of.
  • Fernside. There was a seventy room mansion on Fernside Boulevard and it burned to the ground in 1897 with nobody in it.
  • Gold Coast. The name is not marketing.
  • Harbor Bay Isle. Harbor Bay Isle was supposed to be ten thousand homes.
  • Harbor Bay. Harbor Bay is the half of the Bay Farm fill that was built for work instead of for living, and the ferry is the reason anyone commutes from it.
  • Marina Village. Bethlehem Steel built ships on this ground from 1916 to 1948.
  • Park Street District. The reason downtown Alameda is here is that a train stopped here in 1864.
  • South Shore. This neighborhood did not exist before November 1955.
  • Webster Street District. Webster Street is the West End's main street, and it has had two completely different lives.
  • West End. For twenty two years there was an amusement park at the end of this neighborhood, and people called it the Coney Island of the West.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical Alameda home and the monthly carry lands near $10,804. That is $129,647 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. For 2026, one-unit financing in Alameda County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Figure $15,011 in transfer tax on a $1,145,869 sale here, at 13.10 dollars per thousand. Custom is to split it, so about $7,505 a side, and who pays is set by the contract.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $17,188.

What waiting costs

The two year cost of waiting, price plus payment, comes to about $56,488 here. The five year figure is $175,964.

This rests on one observed year carried forward. The two year figure is the defensible one; the five year figure is arithmetic, not a forecast.

item.content:encoded:
San Leandro's first settler was a man who had just finished a year running Yerba Buena.

Jose Joaquin Estudillo was born in Monterey in 1800 and served as alcalde of the settlement that became San Francisco. When his term ended he took his wife and ten children across the bay and settled on San Leandro Creek, just outside the Peraltas' Rancho San Antonio, the first settlers in what would be called Eden Township. His grant, Rancho San Leandro, ran from San Leandro Creek south to San Lorenzo Creek. He died in 1852.

The family house went up on what is now West Estudillo Avenue around 1850. California made it Historical Landmark No. 279 in 1938 and it was demolished in 1948. Casa Peralta survives at 384 West Estudillo Avenue, built in 1901 by Ludovino Peralta and on the National Register since January 4, 1982, run today as a city museum.

Two of this city's neighborhoods are named after what came next. Thomas Mulford was a Forty-niner who squatted on the rancho, ignoring the Spanish titles; his hunting led to a bay landing, then a freighting business, then an oyster fishery, and Mulford Gardens carries his name. Daniel Best Agricultural Works gave San Leandro its first large sustained payroll, and Best Manor carries his.

In between, the place was orchards. Cherries were the crop and the city was known as the Cherry City. After the Second World War the cherry orchards and rhubarb fields went under tracts and freeways. That is the San Leandro you see now.

It has 31,954 housing units and 26.2 percent of them predate 1950, so it is older than Hayward next door and far newer than Oakland above it. 57.3 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy is 58.1 percent, the ACS median value is 844,200 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,186.

One question applies everywhere here. The Hayward Fault runs along the hills on this city's eastern edge. Ask the title company whether any parcel you are serious about sits inside an Alquist-Priolo earthquake fault zone, and ask whether the house has ever been bolted.

What the market is doing right now

$798,068 is the typical San Leandro home as of 2026-09-30. Month over month that is up 0.43 percent, and over the year down 0.4 percent.

Listing activity in San Leandro for 2026-09. Active inventory is 74, down 1.4 percent from the prior month and down 22.3 percent from a year earlier. 48 new listings came on, up 0.0 percent month over month, and 43 went pending. Median days on market is 35, up 28.6 percent month over month and up 8.3 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $844,472 at $539 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,532 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,875.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $798,068, up 0.43 percent month over month, down 0.4 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $7,779, or $93,344 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 14 areas of San Leandro. What each one actually is:

  • Bal. Bal is one of the smaller named pockets in San Leandro and its published history belongs to the city, so this is that plus the development record.
  • Best Manor. Best Manor is named after the man who gave San Leandro its first real payroll.
  • Bonaire. Bonaire is a postwar San Leandro neighborhood whose published history is the city's, so this is that plus the development record and the practical read.
  • Broadmoor. Broadmoor is one of San Leandro's established residential neighborhoods on the older side of the city, and its story is the city's.
  • Davis Tract. Davis Tract takes its name from the subdivision that created it.
  • Dayton. Dayton is a central San Leandro neighborhood with little published history of its own, so this is the city's record and the practical read.
  • Downtown. San Leandro's first settler brought his wife and ten children across the bay and sat down on the creek.
  • Estudillo Estates. This neighborhood is named for the man the whole city traces back to.
  • Farrelly Pond. Farrelly Pond is a small central San Leandro neighborhood named for a body of water, and its published history is the city's.
  • Floresta Gardens. Floresta Gardens is a postwar San Leandro tract and the name is the only decorative thing about it.
  • Halcyon Foothill. Halcyon and Foothill are the two roads this neighborhood is named for, running along the eastern side of San Leandro where the ground starts to rise.
  • Heron Bay. Heron Bay is the newest ground in San Leandro, out at the shoreline, and that position is the entire brief.
  • Mulford Gardens. Thomas Mulford turned up during the Gold Rush, ignored the Spanish land titles, and settled on the rancho anyway.
  • Washington Manor. Washington Manor is one of San Leandro's big postwar tracts, out on the flat southwestern side of the city, and it is a clean example of what happened to the orchards.

What it costs to own here

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $7,779 monthly, or $93,344 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. The conforming and FHA ceiling for a one-unit property in Alameda County is $1,249,125 in 2026.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical San Leandro home, $798,068, comes to roughly $9,657 at a rate of 12.10 per thousand. Expect it split, near enough $4,828 apiece, with the contract having the final say.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $11,971.

What waiting costs

On the same trailing rate, two years of waiting adds up to roughly -$6,634 in price and payment combined, and five years to -$19,916.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

item.description: What the Hayward housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $816,424, up 0.13 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Hayward called itself the Apricot City, and it meant it.

The town incorporated on March 11, 1876 under the name Haywards, with an s, taken from the hotel the settlement had grown around. What made it was fruit. From the second half of the nineteenth century this was one of California's leading fruit growing districts, sending cherries, apricots, peaches, tomatoes and potatoes out by rail. Hunt Brothers opened a cannery here in 1895 and ran it as a seasonal industry large enough to build worker cottages and community buildings around itself. By 1950 the city had about 14,000 residents.

Two other stories sit in that landscape. In 1918 Zenjuro Shibata moved out from Oakland and founded Mt. Eden Nursery on a marshy plot, recorded in his eldest son Yoshio's name because California law then barred him from holding it in his own. The first greenhouse went up that year in carnations and the family switched to roses in the mid 1930s. The nursery ran into the 1980s and the Shibata Garden at 25941 Industrial Boulevard is what remains of it. And out on the bay flats there was a separate community called Russell City, named in the 1850s or laid out in 1907 depending on which account you take. The county removed it by eminent domain by 1964 and put an industrial park on the ground.

After the Second World War the orchards went under tracts, and that is the city you see now. Hayward has 52,243 housing units and only 9.1 percent of them predate 1950, so this is overwhelmingly a postwar place. 51.2 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy is 58.0 percent, the ACS median value is 854,400 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,391.

One thing applies everywhere here and nowhere else so strongly. The Hayward Fault runs the length of this city. Ask the title company whether any parcel you are serious about sits inside an Alquist-Priolo earthquake fault zone, and ask whether the house has ever been bolted to its foundation. In Hayward that is the first question, not the last.

What the market is doing right now

  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 18 areas of Hayward. What each one actually is:

  • Burbank. Burbank is one of Hayward's older central neighborhoods, close in to downtown, and the published history belongs to the city, not the pocket, so this is that history plus the development record.
  • Downtown Hayward. The city was incorporated on March 11, 1876 under the name Haywards, with the s, and it was named after a hotel.
  • Eden Shores. Eden Shores is the newest ground in Hayward and it sits out on the bay edge.
  • Fairview Hills. Fairview Hills is on the unincorporated slope above Hayward, and that word unincorporated is the practical headline.
  • Fairway Park. Fairway Park is postwar Hayward out toward the bay side, laid out around a golf course, and the name is literal.
  • Glen Eden. Eden is the old name for this whole area.
  • Harder Tennyson. Harder and Tennyson are the two roads this neighborhood is named for, in the southern part of Hayward, and the history here is the city's.
  • Hayward Highland. Hayward Highland sits on the slope above the city with the Hayward Fault running along the foot of it.
  • Hayward Hills. The Hayward Fault runs along the base of these hills, and it is the reason there are hills here at all.
  • Jackson Triangle. Jackson Triangle takes its name from its shape, wedged between Jackson Street and the streets that cut across it in central Hayward.
  • Longwood Winton Grove. Longwood and Winton Grove sit either side of Winton Avenue in central Hayward, and like most of this city the neighborhood's story is the city's story.
  • Mission Garin. Mission Boulevard runs along the foot of the hills here and Garin Regional Park is immediately above, and the neighborhood is named for both.
  • Mt Eden. In 1918 a man named Zenjuro Shibata moved out from Oakland and started a nursery here.
  • Prospect Hill. Prospect Hill is one of Hayward's older residential pockets on the rise just east of downtown, and the name describes exactly what it is.
  • Santa Clara. The Santa Clara neighborhood sits in central Hayward and its published history is the city's, so this is that plus the development record and the buying read.
  • Southgate. Southgate is postwar south Hayward and its history is the city's, so this is that plus the development record and the practical read.
  • Tennyson Alquire. Tennyson and Alquire are the two roads at the centre of this south Hayward neighborhood, and the published history belongs to the city, not the pocket.
  • The Cannery. The neighborhood is named after a cannery and the cannery is the reason Hayward existed as an economy.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $7,938 a month, $95,260 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Figure $7,838 in transfer tax on a $816,424 sale here, at 9.60 dollars per thousand. It is normally split down the middle, about $3,919 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $12,246.

What waiting costs

The two year cost of waiting, price plus payment, comes to about -$44,655 here. The five year figure is -$130,051.

One year of data, extended. That is worth saying plainly, because compounding it out to five years makes the total look more certain than it is.

item.title: Fremont: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Fremont housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,439,805, up 0.08 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Fremont is five towns that agreed to become one city on January 23, 1956, and it still reads that way on the ground.

Mission San Jose, Centerville, Niles, Irvington and Warm Springs each had their own main street, their own cemetery and their own reason for existing before the merger. Wally Pond, a former councilmember, is the one who got it through. Washington Township had organized the area back in 1853. Newark was asked to join, its voters declined, and it incorporated separately in 1955. The city took its name from John C. Fremont, who mapped a route through Mission Pass into the rest of the bay.

The result is a city that does not have one center. It has five, and the distance between them is why a buyer who has only looked at Fremont on a map tends to be surprised in person. Old Mission San Jose, at 43300 Mission Boulevard, was founded on June 11, 1797 and keeps the oldest standing adobe building in Alameda County, put up in 1809. Niles has a pre war commercial street and the studio ground where Charlie Chaplin shot five films in 1915. Warm Springs has what is left of the winery Leland Stanford bought in 1869 and his brother Josiah built out to 350 acres. Centerville has a cemetery from 1855 with the road names buried in it. Ardenwood has a redwood farmhouse from 1857 with an 1889 Queen Anne addition by Samuel Newsom.

The modern economy sits at the south end. General Motors opened Fremont Assembly in 1963, closed it in 1982, reopened it with Toyota as NUMMI in 1984, and that venture built more than eight million vehicles before Toyota shut it in April 2010 and 4,700 people lost their jobs. Tesla reopened it that October and built close to 560,000 vehicles there in 2023.

So treat Fremont as five housing markets instead of one. The year built swings from mission era ground to current construction, sometimes within a mile, and the inspection list, the tax bill and the commute are all different in each of the five. Pick the district first and the house second. And drive your actual commute, at your actual hour, before you decide which of the five you can live in.

What the market is doing right now

Measured to 2026-09-30, typical value in Fremont is $1,439,805: up 0.08 percent against last month, down 1.5 percent against last year.

Listing activity in Fremont for 2026-09. Median days on market is 31, down 0.7 percent month over month and down 11.3 percent year over year.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,439,805, up 0.08 percent month over month, down 1.5 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $13,361, or $160,327 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 19 areas of Fremont. What each one actually is:

  • Ardenwood. A Pennsylvania farmer named George Washington Patterson came to California for gold in 1849, found almost none, and in 1857 built a redwood farmhouse here instead.
  • Baylands. This is the edge of Fremont where the city stops and the bay starts, and most of it is federally protected.
  • Brookvale. Brookvale is one of the Fremont neighborhoods where the published history is genuinely thin, so this is the development record and the practical read, not a story somebody made up.
  • Cabrillo. Cabrillo is a 1960s tract neighborhood in north Fremont, and the useful facts about it are in the development record instead of in any story.
  • Centerville. There is a cemetery at Post Street and Bonde Way that is older than the city around it by a century.
  • Cherry Guardino. Cherry-Guardino takes its name from its two main streets, and like several Fremont tract neighborhoods it has almost no published history.
  • City Center. On September 6, 1960 the Fremont City Council picked the Fudenna ranch as the site for its civic center.
  • Glenmoor. Glenmoor has a homeowners association that was incorporated in March 1953, when there were no more than 75 houses standing in the whole subdivision.
  • Grimmer. Grimmer is named for a family nobody has documented properly, and the honest thing is to say so.
  • Irvington. In 1884 a man named Juan Gallegos built a winery here that was designed to work by gravity.
  • Kimber Gomes. This neighborhood is named after a chicken farm and a school board member, and the chicken farm was world famous.
  • Mission San Jose. The oldest standing adobe building in Alameda County is in this neighborhood, and it has been there since 1809.
  • Mission Valley. Mission Valley is the ground between the old mission and the valley floor, and it was built as housing tracts in the late 1960s.
  • Niles. Charlie Chaplin made five pictures on one block of Niles Boulevard, and you can still sit in a building there and watch them.
  • Northgate. Northgate is a north Fremont neighborhood with very little documented history of its own, so this is the development record and the practical read.
  • Parkmont. Parkmont is a postwar tract neighborhood in central Fremont, and what distinguishes it is the mix of what got built instead of any single story.
  • Sundale. Sundale has very little published history, so what follows is the development record and the buying read.
  • Warm Springs. Leland Stanford bought a resort here in 1869 and his brother turned it into a winery that held half a million gallons.
  • Weibel. The name on this neighborhood came off a wine label.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $13,361 a month, $160,327 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

As of 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed averages 7.4 percent, up or down from 6.27 percent twelve months before. The conforming and FHA ceiling for a one-unit property in Alameda County is $1,249,125 in 2026.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical Fremont home, $1,439,805, comes to roughly $1,584 at a rate of 1.10 per thousand. Local practice splits it down the middle, roughly $792 each, though the contract decides.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $21,597.

What waiting costs

Waiting two years at this place's own trailing rate costs about -$49,092, counting the price increase and the payment increase together. Over five years it is -$144,921.

One year of data, extended. That is worth saying plainly, because compounding it out to five years makes the total look more certain than it is.

item.description: What the Newark housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,185,129, down 0.08 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Newark is a separate city because its chamber of commerce refused to be somebody else's industrial zone.

Newark is named after a castle in Scotland. J. Barr Robertson gave it the name, taken from Newark Castle at Port Glasgow. A company bought the land from Washington Township in 1878 to lay the town out, and before that, in 1853, Mayhew's Landing here held warehouses for wheat, hay and coal. The city came much later and it came by refusal: when the five townships around it were merging into Fremont, Newark's Chamber of Commerce objected to being zoned mainly for industry inside that new city and pushed to incorporate on its own instead. Newark became a city on September 22, 1955, the first new city in Alameda County in 47 years. Fremont incorporated four months later without it. That is why a city of 16,015 housing units sits inside the shape of a much larger one.

That refusal is not a quirk. It is the organising fact of the place. Newark kept its own zoning authority specifically so it could decide how much of itself would be industrial, and the result is a city where industrial ground and housing sit closer together than in most of this county.

Newark has 16,015 housing units and 4.5 percent of them predate 1950. 67.9 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 69.4 percent, the ACS median value is 1,142,800 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,776. 67.9 percent single family detached and 69.4 percent owner occupancy are both high, so this is a city of houses.

So three things to do here, in order.

Pull the zoning for the parcel and for everything touching it, and ask the city what is permitted next door instead of looking at what operates there now. In Newark that question has more weight than almost anywhere, for the reason above.

Get the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote before your contingencies expire, because this is flat ground at the bay margin and the premium is a monthly number instead of a closing detail.

Then the house, matched to its year built. Outside Old Town almost everything is postwar, so the list is the roof, the supply lines, the electrical panel capacity, the sewer lateral, the furnace and the water heater, plus the lot dimensions and setbacks if an accessory dwelling unit is in your plan.

What the market is doing right now

The value index puts a typical Newark home at $1,185,129 on 2026-09-30, down 0.08 percent month over month and down 2.4 percent year over year.

Listing activity in Newark for 2026-09. Active inventory is 83, up 13.0 percent from the prior month and up 24.1 percent from a year earlier. 52 new listings came on, up 30.0 percent month over month, and 35 went pending. Median days on market is 29, down 5.0 percent month over month and down 8.1 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $1,198,000 at $692 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,632 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $3,670.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,185,129, down 0.08 percent month over month, down 2.4 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $11,145, or $133,745 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 5 areas of Newark. What each one actually is:

  • Birch Grove. Birch Grove is a postwar Newark neighborhood on the city's flat ground.
  • Bridgepointe. Bridgepointe is one of Newark's later planned developments.
  • Cherry Thornton. Cherry and Thornton are the two streets this Newark neighborhood is named for.
  • Lakeshore. Lakeshore is one of Newark's planned residential neighborhoods, laid out around water features on the flat bay side of the city.
  • Old Town Newark. Newark exists as a separate city because its chamber of commerce did not want to be the industrial zone of somebody else's town.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $11,145 a month, $133,745 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Alameda County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical Newark home, $1,185,129, comes to roughly $1,304 at a rate of 1.10 per thousand. It is normally split down the middle, about $652 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $17,777.

What waiting costs

The two year cost of waiting, price plus payment, comes to about -$64,164 here. The five year figure is -$186,938.

This rests on one observed year carried forward. The two year figure is the defensible one; the five year figure is arithmetic, not a forecast.

item.title: Union City: the October 2026 read

item.content:encoded:
Union City is two nineteenth century towns that agreed in 1959 to stop being annexed.

The Horner brothers made the first non-native settlement here in 1850. Henry C. Smith founded New Haven in 1851, and in 1853 New Haven combined with the nearby town of Alvarado and became the county seat of the newly created Alameda County. Alvarado carries the name of Governor Juan Alvarado, the same governor who granted Guillermo Castro the rancho that became Castro Valley. In 1870 the California Beet Sugar Company opened at Alvarado and ran until 1873, the first successful sugar beet factory in the United States. Ezra Decoto sold land to the railroad, in 1867 by one account and 1870 by another, and the settlement that grew there took his name.

By the 1950s both Alvarado and Decoto were facing absorption by Hayward. A citizens committee petitioned to incorporate instead, the two towns voted together in January 1959, with sources giving January 13 for the vote and January 26 for the incorporation, and Tom Kitayama, who had sat on that committee, became the first mayor.

So the city is sixty odd years old and the places inside it are a hundred and seventy. That shows in the housing.

Union City has 21,901 housing units and 4.0 percent of them predate 1950. 57.8 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 64.7 percent, the ACS median value is 1,104,900 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,713. Only 4.0 percent predates 1950, and almost all of that is in Old Alvarado and Decoto.

That gives you a simple rule for shopping here. Pull the year built first. In the old districts you are buying a pre war building with the full inspection list and a legal unit count worth confirming with the city. Everywhere else you are buying consistent postwar tract housing where the comparable sales genuinely compare and the price spread is condition.

Two things apply across the whole city. It is flat ground near the bay, so get the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote before your contingencies expire. And the Union City BART station is the single largest factor in what an address is worth here, so walk to it from the front door and time it at the hour you would really be walking.

What the market is doing right now

Measured to 2026-09-30, typical value in Union City is $1,195,668: down 0.11 percent against last month, down 1.9 percent against last year.

Listing activity in Union City for 2026-09. Active inventory is 61, up 19.6 percent from the prior month and up 24.5 percent from a year earlier. 40 new listings came on, up 66.7 percent month over month, and 22 went pending. Median days on market is 35, down 2.1 percent month over month and up 28.7 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $1,249,972 at $737 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,534 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,913.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,195,668, down 0.11 percent month over month, down 1.9 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $11,237, or $134,845 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 6 areas of Union City. What each one actually is:

  • Alvarado. Alvarado was the county seat of Alameda County, and it held that job from 1853.
  • Decoto. Decoto is named for a man who sold land to a railroad.
  • Kings Court. Kings Court is one of Union City's postwar residential developments.
  • New Haven. New Haven is the name Henry C.
  • Old Alvarado. Old Alvarado is the surviving nineteenth century core of a city that was not incorporated until 1959.
  • Verona. Verona is a Union City neighborhood built in the city's postwar expansion.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $11,237 a month to own the typical home in Union City, $134,845 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. In Alameda County the 2026 one-unit limit is $1,249,125. It serves as the conforming conventional ceiling and the FHA ceiling at once.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Figure $1,315 in transfer tax on a $1,195,668 sale here, at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Convention puts about $658 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $17,935.

What waiting costs

On the same trailing rate, two years of waiting adds up to roughly -$52,718 in price and payment combined, and five years to -$154,610.

The input is a single trailing year, projected. It is not a forecast, and the five year number is the one to distrust first.

item.content:encoded:
Dublin has three nineteenth century buildings and they are all on the same corner.

The Murray Schoolhouse opened in 1856 with fifty pupils. The Dublin Pioneer Cemetery was formally established in 1859. Green's Store opened in 1860. All three sit at what is now Dublin Boulevard and Donlon Way, and together they are effectively the city's entire pre modern built history.

How they got there starts with a grant. Jose Maria Amador received over 16,000 acres in 1835 for his service as a Mexican soldier and as administrator at Mission San Jose, and the Amador Valley carries his name. Michael Murray and Jeremiah Fallon arrived in 1846 and bought 982 acres from him in the 1850s with money made in the Gold Rush. Murray Township was created in June 1853 and named for Murray, a few months after Alameda County itself was formed. James Witt Dougherty bought 10,000 acres from Amador and became the largest landowner in the area. Two of those names are on the map today: Fallon Village, and Dougherty Road.

Then the valley sat. Dublin did not incorporate as a city until February 1982. That makes it the newest city in Alameda County, and almost everything you can see was built after that.

The figures say it plainly. Dublin has 25,157 housing units and 0.8 percent of them predate 1950, the lowest share anywhere in these three counties. 54.2 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy is 65.7 percent, the ACS median value is 1,317,100 dollars and the median gross rent is 3,191.

So the questions here are not the questions anywhere else in this series. There is no knob and tube wiring to find and no sewer lateral ordinance to budget for. What there is instead is the homeowners association and the tax bill.

Get the association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure. Then pull the actual tax bill for the address, because community facilities district assessments ride on top of the base rate across this city and they are easy to miss until the first bill arrives.

What the market is doing right now

$1,227,704 is the typical Dublin home as of 2026-09-30. Month over month that is down 0.36 percent, and over the year down 5.5 percent.

  • Downtown Dublin. The oldest things in Dublin sit at the corner of Dublin Boulevard and Donlon Way, and there are three of them.
  • Dublin Ranch. Dublin Ranch is the largest of the master planned communities that turned east Dublin from open land into a suburb.
  • East Dublin. East Dublin is the reason this city grew from a crossroads to a suburb inside one generation.
  • Fallon Village. Fallon Village carries the name of Jeremiah Fallon, who arrived in this valley in 1846 and bought 982 acres from Jose Maria Amador in the 1850s with Gold Rush money.
  • Jordan Ranch. Jordan Ranch is one of the named communities in east Dublin, developed as part of the city's continuing eastern build out.
  • Positano. Positano is one of the master planned villages on Dublin's eastern side, built as part of the city's recent expansion.
  • Schaefer Ranch. Schaefer Ranch sits on the western hillside edge of Dublin, above the freeway, and it is one of the city's later developments.
  • Tassajara Hills. Tassajara Hills sits on the rising ground at Dublin's northeastern edge, where the city runs up against open hills.
  • Wallis Ranch. Wallis Ranch is one of the later master planned communities on Dublin's eastern side.
  • West Dublin. West Dublin is the older half of a city that is itself only incorporated since February 1982.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical Dublin home and the monthly carry lands near $11,516. That is $138,189 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

Hold off two years and the combined price and payment cost is near -$151,741. At five years it reaches -$422,060.
