item.description: What the Pleasanton housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,500,493, down 0.01 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Pleasanton is spelled wrong, and it has been since 1894.

The city incorporated on June 18, 1894 and took its name from Major General Alfred Pleasonton of the Union Army. His name has an o in the middle. The town's does not. Nobody fixed it.

Before the name there was a rancho. Rancho el Valle de San Jose was granted in 1839 to the Bernal brothers and their brothers-in-law, and the settlement here was called Alisal in the 1850s when it worked as a mercantile stop on the Gold Rush road. In 1858 the Bernal family built a one-mile racetrack that is still the oldest in the country. John Kottinger is credited by most historians with founding the town: the railroad was announced in 1862, he began selling plots along the planned route the next year, and by 1869 there was a town with the transcontinental line through it. Kottinger is also credited with establishing the first commercial vineyards and winery in Alameda County here in the 1850s. At one point this valley was among the largest hop producers in the world.

Kottinger Ranch carries his name today, up on the hillside above the town he sold the first lots in.

What the city is now is new. Pleasanton has 28,975 housing units and only 2.5 percent of them predate 1950, so almost everything here is postwar or later. 61.1 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy is 67.0 percent, the ACS median value is 1,537,100 dollars and the median gross rent is 3,060.

So treat Pleasanton as two markets. Downtown, where the old street and the old housing are and where the walkability premium sits. And the tracts and hillside developments, where the stock is consistent, the comparable sales actually compare, and the variables are the homeowners association, the tax bill with its district assessments, and on the slopes the soils and the fire insurance.

Pull the year built, then the tax bill, then the association documents. In that order.

What the market is doing right now

Pleasanton sits at $1,500,493 in typical value as of 2026-09-30, having moved down 0.01 percent since last month and down 3.0 percent since last year.

Listing activity in Pleasanton for 2026-09. Active inventory is 110, down 8.8 percent from the prior month and down 3.6 percent from a year earlier. 58 new listings came on, up 3.1 percent month over month, and 43 went pending. Median days on market is 33, down 2.7 percent month over month and down 10.6 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $1,433,972 at $735 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,782 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $3,219.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,500,493, down 0.01 percent month over month, down 3.0 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $13,888, or $166,662 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 12 areas of Pleasanton. What each one actually is:

  • Birdland. Birdland takes its name from its streets.
  • Del Prado. Del Prado is a postwar Pleasanton tract and its published history is the city's, so this is that plus the development record.
  • Downtown Pleasanton. The town is spelled wrong on purpose, or at least it has been since 1894.
  • Golden Eagle. Golden Eagle sits on the hillside ground at the edge of Pleasanton, built late and built large.
  • Kottinger Ranch. This neighborhood is named for the man who sold the first lots in Pleasanton.
  • Laguna Oaks. Laguna Oaks is one of Pleasanton's later hillside developments, built large on big lots.
  • Mohr Martin. Mohr and Martin are the two roads this neighborhood is named for, on the flatter western side of Pleasanton.
  • Pleasanton Meadows. Pleasanton Meadows is a postwar tract on the valley floor and the name is as literal as it sounds.
  • Ruby Hill. Ruby Hill is a gated development on vineyard ground, and the vineyard part is older than almost anything else in this valley.
  • Val Vista. Val Vista is a postwar Pleasanton neighborhood on the valley floor, and its history belongs to the city, not the pocket.
  • Valley Trails. Valley Trails sits on the western side of Pleasanton near the arroyo, and its history is the city's.
  • Vintage Hills. Vintage Hills is named for the vineyards, and the vineyards are the oldest commercial thing in this valley.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical Pleasanton home and the monthly carry lands near $13,888. That is $166,662 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

As of 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed averages 7.4 percent, up or down from 6.27 percent twelve months before. The conforming and FHA ceiling for a one-unit property in Alameda County is $1,249,125 in 2026.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Pleasanton charges 1.10 per thousand, so the typical $1,500,493 home owes roughly $1,651 at transfer. Convention puts about $825 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Emeryville at 26.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $37,512.

What waiting costs

Price and payment together, a two year wait here runs about -$102,628. Stretch it to five and the figure is -$296,196.

Treat it as a scenario, not a prediction. The appreciation input is one year of observed change carried forward, and five years of compounding on one year of data flatters the result.

item.title: Livermore: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Livermore housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,071,869, up 0.03 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Livermore was registered as a town on November 4, 1869, and the man who laid it out named it after a friend.

William Mendenhall founded it that year, once the Central Pacific railroad had reached the valley, and he named it for Robert Livermore. Livermore and Jose Noriega had secured Rancho Las Positas in 1839, and the city sits partly on that grant. There had been a settlement before his: Laddsville, grown up around a hotel Alphonso Ladd opened in the 1860s. The city incorporated on April 1, 1876. The Mendenhall neighborhood carries the founder's name.

Then the valley found the thing it is still known for. In the 1880s Wente, Concannon and Wetmore were doing work here that shaped the California wine industry, and the Livermore Valley has been a wine region continuously since. The vineyards are still working, mostly on the southern side of the city and along Vineyard Avenue.

After the Second World War it became something else again, when the Lawrence Livermore and Sandia national laboratories put a research economy on top of a farming one.

Livermore has 31,936 housing units and 4.5 percent of them predate 1950. 69.2 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy is 72.0 percent. That combination, overwhelmingly detached and overwhelmingly owner occupied, makes this the most straightforward single family market in the three counties. The comparable sales compare, the stock is consistent, and the price spread is mostly condition.

Two things here that do not apply further west. The summer heat is real, so ask the age and running cost of the cooling system on any house. This report covers 10 areas of Livermore. What each one actually is:

  • Downtown Livermore. Livermore was platted and registered on November 4, 1869, and the man who laid it out named it after a friend.
  • Dunsmuir. Dunsmuir is one of Livermore's residential pockets with little published history of its own.
  • Granada. Granada is a postwar Livermore neighborhood whose record is the city's, not its own.
  • Mendenhall. This neighborhood is named for the man who founded the city.
  • North Livermore. North Livermore is the ground north of the old railroad grid, and its record is the city's.

item.content:encoded:
A man named Guillermo Castro gambled away a valley, and the valley kept his name.

Guillermo Castro received Rancho San Lorenzo from Governor Juan Alvarado. Most sources date the grant to 1841 and one book on the valley says 1843, and the size is given as either 26,722 acres or about 28,000. It covered what is now Hayward, San Lorenzo and Castro Valley, taking in Crow Canyon, Cull Canyon and Palomares Canyon. Castro gambled. He sold off pieces of the rancho to cover his debts, mortgaged what was left, and fought lawsuits from Gold Rush settlers trying to clear squatters. In 1864 the sheriff, I. A. Mayhew, presided over the sale of the last of it for 400,000 dollars to Faxon Atherton.

That is the whole nineteenth century here in one story, and the ground Castro lost is now Hayward, San Lorenzo and Castro Valley.

The twentieth century fact that matters more to a buyer is administrative. Castro Valley is the largest community in unincorporated Alameda County. There is no city hall, no city council and no city planning department. Alameda County issues the permits, sets the zoning and provides most of the services, and there have been repeated efforts over the years to incorporate it as a city or annex it to Hayward or San Leandro, none of which took.

Castro Valley has 22,957 housing units and 16.9 percent of them predate 1950. 73.3 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 72.5 percent, both high for this series. The ACS median value is 1,104,600 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,554. That 73.3 percent detached figure and 72.5 percent owner occupancy are both high for this series, and they describe a valley of houses instead of apartments.

So three things here that do not apply the same way elsewhere.

Confirm jurisdiction. The county, not a city, answers your permit and zoning questions, and you should ask directly what services come with a specific address.

Ask the fault question. The Hayward Fault runs along the western edge of this valley. Ask the title company whether a parcel sits inside an Alquist-Priolo earthquake fault zone, and ask whether the house has ever been bolted.

And on the canyon and hillside ground, a large share of this valley, ask for the soils and drainage history, the condition and ownership of any retaining structures, and a written fire insurance quote on the exact address.

  • Jensen Ranch. Jensen Ranch is hillside development on the ridge above Castro Valley, built late and built large.

  • Palomares Hills. Palomares Hills sits above the valley in one of the canyons that was part of Guillermo Castro's rancho, and the canyon still carries the Palomares name.

  • The Village. San Lorenzo Village is one of the clearest examples of a planned wartime and postwar community anywhere in this series.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $7,784 a month, $93,413 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

item.title: Sunol: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Sunol housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,417,745, up 0.51 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Sunol has 330 housing units. That is not a typo and it is the most important number on this page.

The place sits in the hills between Fremont and Pleasanton, unincorporated, in the valley the regional water system runs through. 97.3 percent of its housing is single family detached, among the highest shares anywhere in this series. 43.6 percent predates 1950. Owner occupancy is 82.1 percent and the ACS median value is 1,333,300 dollars.

One thing does run through Sunol, and it is a railway. The Niles Canyon Railway operates on the original alignment of the First Transcontinental Railroad, the eleven mile section between Sunol and the Niles district of Fremont. The National Register listed that stretch on October 13, 2010 as the Niles Canyon Transcontinental Railroad Historic District. The Pacific Locomotive Association leased the right of way and began rebuilding track in 1987, and the first passenger train ran out of Sunol on May 21, 1988. Trains still run it.

So the valley that holds 330 homes also holds the western end of the line that first connected California to the rest of the country, and the depot is a short walk from most of the housing.

A place this small does not behave like a market. In a normal month there may be no sales at all. That means comparable sales are frequently unavailable, and any index or automated valuation built on this little transaction volume should be treated with real caution instead of quoted as fact. Pricing here reasons from the land and the condition, not from a recent sale down the street, because there usually is not one.

So the work is land work.

Establish jurisdiction: Sunol is unincorporated, so Alameda County handles planning and permits, and you should ask exactly which services come with the address.

Ask about water and waste. Whether the parcel is on a well or district water, and if a well, the yield and the water quality testing. Whether there is a septic system, when it was last inspected and when it was last pumped.

Ask about access. Whether the road to the property is public or private, and if private, who maintains it and under what recorded agreement, because that obligation transfers with the land.

Then get a written fire insurance quote on the exact address early, with the risk rating explained. In a small valley ringed by open hills, that number can decide the purchase.

What the market is doing right now

Typical home value in Sunol is $1,417,745 as of 2026-09-30, up 0.51 percent from the month before and up 3.2 percent over the year.

Listing activity in Sunol for 2026-09. Active inventory is 9, up 12.5 percent from the prior month and up 125.0 percent from a year earlier. 2 new listings came on, and 1 went pending. Median days on market is 73, up 36.8 percent month over month and down 1.4 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $1,199,500 at $751 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,700 square feet.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,417,745, up 0.51 percent month over month, up 3.2 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $13,169, or $158,025 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 1 area of Sunol. What each one actually is:

  • Sunol. Sunol has 330 housing units in total.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical Sunol home and the monthly carry lands near $13,169. That is $158,025 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

As of 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed averages 7.4 percent, up or down from 6.27 percent twelve months before. Alameda County's 2026 one-unit loan limit sits at $1,249,125. That is the cap for conforming conventional and for FHA alike.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Sunol charges 1.10 per thousand, so the typical $1,417,745 home owes roughly $1,560 at transfer. It is normally split down the middle, about $780 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $21,266.

What waiting costs

Hold off two years and the combined price and payment cost is near $105,892. At five years it reaches $335,199.

The input is a single trailing year, projected. It is not a forecast, and the five year number is the one to distrust first.

item.title: Richmond: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Richmond housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $600,691, up 0.28 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Richmond was a refinery before it was a city.

Standard Oil built here in 1901, with one account giving 1902, and by 1904 the plant was reported as the second largest oil refinery in the world. Chevron runs it today. The city incorporated in 1905, four years after the refinery.

The railroad came first of all. The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe put its western terminus at Point Richmond, in 1899 by one source and on July 4, 1900 by another, and ran ferries across to San Francisco. The settlement there was called East Yards before it was called Point Richmond, and it served as the city's downtown into the early 1900s. Ford opened an assembly plant in 1930.

Then the war. This is what Richmond is known for. Henry Kaiser opened his first shipyard here in December 1940. The city had fewer than 24,000 people that year and nearly 100,000 by 1943. Four yards built 747 ships, more than any other shipyard complex in the country. The Rosie the Riveter World War II Home Front National Historical Park was dedicated on October 25, 2000, the first national park created to commemorate the home front, and the SS Red Oak Victory is moored on the waterfront where the yards stood.

Richmond has 42,509 housing units and 28.5 percent of them predate 1950, the highest share of any city in this county with more than 20,000 housing units. 59.9 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy is 54.7 percent, and the ACS median value is 668,200 dollars.

So this is really two markets. The flats and the older neighborhoods, where the housing is pre war, the inspection list is long, and the zoning question matters because industry runs through them. And the waterfront, built on former shipyard ground, where the stock is new, the associations are the asset you are buying alongside the house, and the environmental record for the parcel is the first document to ask for.

Pull the year built. It tells you which Richmond you are in.

What the market is doing right now

$600,691 is the typical Richmond home as of 2026-09-30. Month over month that is up 0.28 percent, and over the year down 1.0 percent.

Listing activity in Richmond for 2026-09. Active inventory is 115, down 2.4 percent from the prior month and down 19.6 percent from a year earlier. 54 new listings came on, up 0.0 percent month over month, and 66 went pending. Median days on market is 30, down 22.4 percent month over month and down 11.0 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $560,113 at $509 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,216 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,565.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $600,691, up 0.28 percent month over month, down 1.0 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $6,007, or $72,082 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 22 areas of Richmond. What each one actually is:

  • Atchison Village. Atchison Village was built to house the people building ships.
  • Belding Woods. Belding and Woods are the two names this central Richmond neighborhood carries.
  • Brickyard Cove. Brickyard Cove is named for what used to be here, and the shoreline is the whole reason to buy.
  • Carriage Hills. Carriage Hills is hill ground on Richmond's eastern edge.
  • Clinton Hill. Clinton Hill is on the rising eastern side of Richmond.
  • Coronado. Coronado is one of Richmond's older flatland neighborhoods, south of the city centre.
  • Cortez Stege. Cortez and Stege are the two names on this neighborhood at the southern end of Richmond.
  • East Richmond Heights. East Richmond Heights sits on the slope above the city, and part of it is unincorporated county ground.
  • Fairmede Hilltop. Fairmede and Hilltop are the two names on this neighborhood in north Richmond, near the Hilltop commercial district.
  • Hilltop District. The Hilltop district is north Richmond's commercial centre and the housing built around it.
  • Iron Triangle. The name comes from the railroads.
  • May Valley. May Valley sits in the eastern hills of Richmond, where the city runs up against open ground.
  • Metro Village. Metro Village sits near the Richmond transit corridor on the city's central flats.
  • Parchester Village. Parchester Village is a planned postwar community at the northern edge of Richmond, laid out as a single development with its own street pattern and its own community organisation.
  • Park Plaza. Park Plaza is one of Richmond's central residential neighborhoods.
  • Point Richmond. A railroad picked this spot and the city grew around it afterward.
  • Pullman. Pullman takes its name from the railroad car company.
  • Richmond Annex. The Richmond Annex is the southern tip of the city, pressed up against the El Cerrito line.
  • Richmond Heights. Richmond Heights sits on the rising ground on the eastern side of the city.
  • Richmond View. Richmond View is on the hill ground at the eastern edge of the city, above the flats.
  • Santa Fe. This neighborhood is named for the railroad that made the city.
  • Shields Reid. Shields and Reid are the two names this north Richmond neighborhood carries.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $6,007 a month, $72,082 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. The conforming and FHA ceiling for a one-unit property in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125 in 2026.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Richmond charges 8.10 per thousand, so the typical $600,691 home owes roughly $4,866 at transfer. It is normally split down the middle, about $2,433 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. At $1,000,000 the rate steps from 8.10 to 13.50 per thousand, so a sale one dollar over that line pays about $5,400 more than a sale one dollar under it. On anything pricing near $1,000,000, the number to run is not the percentage. It is which side of the line the contract price lands on.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $7,208.

What waiting costs

On the same trailing rate, two years of waiting adds up to roughly -$13,716 in price and payment combined, and five years to -$40,789.

This rests on one observed year carried forward. The two year figure is the defensible one; the five year figure is arithmetic, not a forecast.

The full report

item.content:encoded:
San Pablo kept the rancho's name while the cities around it were carved out of the same grant.

San Pablo carries the name of the rancho. Don Victor Castro's Rancho San Pablo covered this ground and the neighbouring cities were carved out of it, El Cerrito among them, settled after the 1906 earthquake by people leaving San Francisco. San Pablo itself stayed its own place.

San Pablo has 9,943 housing units and 18.4 percent of them predate 1950. 45.1 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 42.0 percent, the lowest owner occupancy rate of any city in this county. The ACS median value is 551,700 dollars and ZHVI is about 554,000, down 0.7 percent over the year.

That 42.0 percent owner occupancy is the number to understand here. A majority of the housing in this city is renter occupied, so a buyer is frequently looking at property that has been a rental, and the inspection and the permit history matter more than usual.

So the questions here start with what the property has been. Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, and get the permit history, because conversions and additions without permits are the common problem in a market with this much rental stock. Ask whether the building is nonconforming, since that limits what you can rebuild after a loss.

Pull the year built. 18.4 percent of this stock is pre war, so foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring and galvanized supply lines are live questions on a good share of addresses.

Then pull the zoning for the parcel and everything touching it, and get the tax bill for the address.

And one habit worth keeping in this county. Pull the year built before you form any opinion on a listing, because it decides the entire inspection list and it is the single most useful number on a property profile. Then get the tax bill for the exact address off the county roll, not the listing estimate, and read which districts and assessments are on it. Those two documents cost nothing, they take a day, and between them they settle most of what a buyer actually needs to know before writing an offer.

What the market is doing right now

San Pablo sits at $553,824 in typical value as of 2026-09-30, having moved up 0.24 percent since last month and down 0.7 percent since last year.

Listing activity in San Pablo for 2026-09. Active inventory is 66, down 7.8 percent from the prior month and down 20.6 percent from a year earlier. 30 new listings came on, down 16.7 percent month over month, and 29 went pending. Median days on market is 42, up 9.2 percent month over month and down 2.4 percent year over year.

  • Monthly cost of owning it: $5,603, or $67,242 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 4 areas of San Pablo. What each one actually is:

  • 23rd Street Corridor. The 23rd Street corridor runs through San Pablo and into Richmond, and it is a commercial spine with housing on the streets off it.
  • El Portal. El Portal is a San Pablo neighborhood along the corridor of the same name.
  • Old Town San Pablo. Old Town San Pablo is the original centre, on the rancho ground.
  • Vista Hills. Vista Hills is on the rising ground in San Pablo.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $5,603, $67,242 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical San Pablo home, $553,824, comes to roughly $609 at a rate of 1.10 per thousand. Convention puts about $305 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $6,646.

What waiting costs

Price and payment together, a two year wait here runs about -$8,707. Stretch it to five and the figure is -$26,014.

One year of data, extended. That is worth saying plainly, because compounding it out to five years makes the total look more certain than it is.

item.content:encoded:
El Cerrito was settled by people running from an earthquake, and it was called Rust.

El Cerrito was built by refugees and it was called Rust first. People leaving San Francisco after the 1906 earthquake settled on what was then Don Victor Castro's Rancho San Pablo. The post office opened in 1909 with Rust as the first postmaster on March 1 of that year. The residents disliked the name and changed it to El Cerrito, Little Hill. The village incorporated on August 23, 1917 with about 1,500 people, on a vote of 158 to 131.

The Cerrito Theatre at 10070 San Pablo Avenue opened in 1937 in Art Deco, closed in 1966, and was restored forty years later by the El Cerrito Redevelopment Agency. Victor Castro's adobe stood in the El Cerrito Plaza area until it burned in 1956.

El Cerrito has 11,247 housing units and 32.8 percent of them predate 1950, one of the highest pre war shares in the county. 66.6 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 58.6 percent, and the ACS median value is 1,124,400 dollars. ZHVI is about 1,122,000 dollars, up 3.4 percent over the year.

That 32.8 percent pre war share is the highest of any city in this county, ahead of Richmond, so the inspection list here is a pre war list more often than not.

So pull the year built first. Foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, the original windows and siding. On the hill addresses, soils, drainage, retaining structures and a written fire insurance quote on the exact address.

And note the two BART stations, Plaza and del Norte. Walk to whichever one serves the address and time it yourself, then ask the city about any station area specific plan covering the parcel.

And one habit worth keeping in this county. Pull the year built before you form any opinion on a listing, because it decides the entire inspection list and it is the single most useful number on a property profile. Then get the tax bill for the exact address off the county roll, not the listing estimate, and read which districts and assessments are on it. Those two documents cost nothing, they take a day, and between them they settle most of what a buyer actually needs to know before writing an offer.

What the market is doing right now

As of 2026-09-30 the typical El Cerrito home is worth $1,122,098. That is up 0.76 percent on the month and up 3.4 percent on the year.

Listing activity in El Cerrito for 2026-09. Active inventory is 27, up 8.0 percent from the prior month and up 17.4 percent from a year earlier. 22 new listings came on, up 37.5 percent month over month, and 11 went pending. Median days on market is 23, down 20.2 percent month over month and up 71.7 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $899,000 at $635 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,418 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,597.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,122,098, up 0.76 percent month over month, up 3.4 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $10,494, or $125,932 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 6 areas of El Cerrito. What each one actually is:

  • Cerrito Vista. Cerrito Vista is an El Cerrito neighborhood on the rising ground, near the park of the same name.
  • El Cerrito Del Norte. El Cerrito del Norte is the northern end of the city, around the BART station of that name.
  • El Cerrito Hills. The El Cerrito hills are the upper side of the city, on the slope above San Pablo Avenue.
  • El Cerrito Plaza. El Cerrito Plaza is the southern commercial centre of the city, and Victor Castro's adobe stood on this ground until 1956.
  • Fairmont. Fairmont is a central El Cerrito neighborhood, named like the school.
  • Mira Vista. Mira Vista is a hill neighborhood in El Cerrito, and the name needs care.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $10,494, $125,932 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

The 30-year fixed average is 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent in the same week last year. For 2026, one-unit financing in Contra Costa County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical El Cerrito home, $1,122,098, comes to roughly $14,699 at a rate of 13.10 per thousand. Local practice splits it down the middle, roughly $7,350 each, though the contract decides.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against Richmond at 13.50. Same county, same price, and the spread is $13,914.

What waiting costs

Waiting two years at this place's own trailing rate costs about $89,005, counting the price increase and the payment increase together. Over five years it is $282,565.

Treat it as a scenario, not a prediction. The appreciation input is one year of observed change carried forward, and five years of compounding on one year of data flatters the result.

item.title: Pinole: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Pinole housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $716,435, up 0.52 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Pinole has an 1824 rancho name and almost no nineteenth century housing.

Pinole takes its name from Rancho El Pinole. The Mexican government granted over 17,000 acres including Pinole Creek to Don Ignacio Martinez, commandant of the San Francisco Presidio, in 1823 by one account and 1824 by another, and the same grant covered Alhambra Valley over in Martinez. A Spanish expedition under Don Pedro Fages had come through this part of Contra Costa well before that. Dr. Samuel J. Tennent married Rafaela, Martinez's daughter, and through her inheritance came to control much of the land here. Bernardo Fernandez, who came from Portugal, made a success of a bayside trading operation in the 1850s and built a mansion that still stands at the end of Tennent Avenue.

The railroad arrived in 1878 and opened the waterfront next door to the California Powder Works, at the place they named Hercules. During World War I that plant made more TNT than any other plant in the country. Pinole itself incorporated in 1903. Interstate 80 came through in 1958 and turned the town into a bedroom community, and the downtown still holds much of its turn of the century building stock.

Pinole has 7,056 housing units and only 4.5 percent of them predate 1950, so despite the old name this is largely a postwar city. 74.0 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 79.4 percent, and the ACS median value is 718,600 dollars. ZHVI is about 716,000 dollars, up 0.1 percent over the year.

That 4.5 percent pre war figure is the one to hold onto, because the Old Town name misleads buyers into expecting an older city than this is. Old Town is where the pre war stock is and the rest of Pinole is postwar.

So pull the year built and let it decide the inspection list. On the postwar tracts, the panel, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof and the foundation bolting. In Old Town, the full pre war list plus the zoning and any historic district rules.

On the shoreline side, get the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote. And get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

And one habit worth keeping in this county. Pull the year built before you form any opinion on a listing, because it decides the entire inspection list and it is the single most useful number on a property profile. Hercules is named after dynamite and 0.5 percent of its housing predates 1950.

Hercules is named after dynamite. The California Powder Works developed this site in 1881 to make its patented explosive, Hercules powder, and the town took the product's name. The company's managers incorporated the town itself on December 15, 1900, because they could not get the county supervisors to pass the laws they wanted for the plant. The corporate history is tangled: an earlier Hercules Powder Company was incorporated in 1882 by DuPont with Laflin and Rand and DuPont dissolved it in 1904, and a later one was incorporated on October 18, 1912 and began business in January 1913.

Hercules has 9,581 housing units and 0.5 percent of them predate 1950. For a town incorporated in 1900 that is the whole modern history of the place in one number: almost everything standing here went up long after the powder works. 57.9 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 79.2 percent, and the ACS median value is 769,400 dollars. ZHVI is about 736,000 dollars, down 0.7 percent over the year.

So this is a town with a nineteenth century industrial history and almost entirely modern housing, and those two facts shape different questions.

On the housing, the questions are newer-construction questions. Get the association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure. Get the tax bill for the address and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and when each expires.

On the ground, ask for the site history in writing, because this shoreline manufactured explosives for roughly a century and the record is public. On the shoreline developments, get the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote and ask who maintains any bulkhead or levee the property sits behind.

And in the historic district, read the district rules before planning any exterior change.

item.content:encoded:
Concord was a Mexican land grant, then a town square, then a BART suburb, and it is about to become something else again.

Rancho Monte del Diablo went to Salvio Pacheco in 1834. In 1868 the Pacheco family and Francisco Galindo laid out a town on it called Todos Santos, and the Contra Costa Gazette announced the new name Concord on April 17, 1869. The plaza at the centre is 2.5 acres bounded by Salvio Street, Willow Pass Road, Grant Street and Mount Diablo Street. Sources differ on whether it was dedicated in 1868 or 1869. In 2018 the American Planning Association named it one of three Great Places in California. A number of the historic houses around it were moved there from elsewhere in Concord to save them from demolition.

Then the city filled in fast. Park and Shop and Sun Valley Mall opened as regional shopping destinations through the 1950s and 1960s, BART arrived in 1973, and Joseph Eichler built three tracts here, Rancho Del Diablo, Rancho Los Santos and Parkwood Estates, roughly 175 homes in 1963 and 1964.

Concord also holds a national memorial. On July 17, 1944 at 10:08 at night, an explosion at Port Chicago killed 320 men, the worst stateside disaster of World War II. The trial that followed was the largest naval mutiny case in United States history and it led to the desegregation of the Navy. The Port Chicago Naval Magazine National Memorial was established in 1992 and became a unit of the national park system in 2009. It sits on Suisun Bay on an active military base and can only be visited by reservation.

Concord has 47,703 housing units and 6.7 percent of them predate 1950. 58.7 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 61.6 percent, and the ACS median value is 797,600 dollars. The city's own figure is that 73 percent of its existing homes went up between 1950 and 1979. Citywide ZHVI is about 721,000 dollars, up 0.2 percent over the year.

One thing hangs over every address in this city. The former Concord Naval Weapons Station covers roughly 2,225 acres and the reuse plan calls for more than 12,000 homes, 6 million square feet of commercial space and more than 800 acres of parks, with Brookfield Properties as master developer. The city announced on September 24, 2026 that the Navy had approved the term sheet, and the governor signed SB 328, exempting the project from the Surplus Land Act and streamlining its environmental review. The site is a federal Superfund site with lead and arsenic in it and the Navy has to finish the cleanup before anything gets built. Nobody can tell you the delivery date.

So a buyer in Concord is buying a postwar tract house in a city with a 2,225 acre question mark in it. Pull the year built and the permit history. Get the tax bill for the address. And ask for the base timeline as a range.

What the market is doing right now

$720,907 is the typical Concord home as of 2026-09-30. Month over month that is up 0.37 percent, and over the year up 0.2 percent.

Listing activity in Concord for 2026-09. Active inventory is 203, up 2.7 percent from the prior month and up 0.3 percent from a year earlier. 86 new listings came on, up 3.1 percent month over month, and 70 went pending. Median days on market is 40, up 10.7 percent month over month and down 18.8 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $751,719 at $467 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,396 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,819.

  • Monthly cost of owning it: $7,041, or $84,498 a year, HOA not included.

item.content:encoded:
Walnut Creek was a crossroads called The Corners, and the post office renamed it in 1862.

Walnut Creek was called The Corners until the post office renamed it in 1862. The Southern Pacific arrived in 1891. It became the eighth city in Contra Costa County on October 21, 1914, by a vote of 127 to 67, with a population of about 500 and Harry Spencer as its first board president. One account says the voters wanted incorporation partly so the town could tax itself to pave Main Street. BART arrived in 1973.

The city's best known neighborhood started as a cattle ranch. Stanley Dollar built an estate in Tice Valley in the 1930s, where the family bred Hereford cattle and raised show horses. In 1960 Dollar's son sold it to Ross W. Cortese of the Rossmoor Corporation. Cortese began intending a Leisure World style community and dropped that plan shortly after breaking ground, and Rossmoor opened as a retirement community in 1964. Cortese also built a separate Rossmoor in Orange County between 1955 and 1961, so anybody researching the name needs to check which one a source is about.

Walnut Creek has 34,389 housing units and only 5.3 percent of them predate 1950. 36.8 percent are single family detached, the lowest detached share of any large city in this county. Owner occupancy runs 64.4 percent and the ACS median value is 1,057,300 dollars. Citywide ZHVI is about 990,000 dollars, up 1.3 percent over the year.

That 36.8 percent detached share is the number that explains this market. Walnut Creek has more attached housing and more association governed housing than its neighbours, so in a large share of the city the budget and the reserve study are as much of the purchase as the unit is.

So pull the year built, get the association budget and the reserve study where there is an association, and get the tax bill for the address. In Rossmoor, confirm the age restriction and your lender's willingness to finance there before you do anything else.

What the market is doing right now

$990,472 is the typical Walnut Creek home as of 2026-09-30. Month over month that is up 0.32 percent, and over the year up 1.3 percent.

Listing activity in Walnut Creek for 2026-09. Active inventory is 253, down 0.4 percent from the prior month and up 10.1 percent from a year earlier. 124 new listings came on, up 21.0 percent month over month, and 104 went pending. Median days on market is 37, up 2.0 percent month over month and up 7.7 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $670,250 at $574 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,158 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $3,118.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $990,472, up 0.32 percent month over month, up 1.3 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $9,361, or $112,338 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 12 areas of Walnut Creek. What each one actually is:

  • Downtown. Downtown Walnut Creek is the commercial centre of central Contra Costa County, and the street at the middle of it is the reason the city incorporated.
  • Indian Valley. Indian Valley is a residential neighborhood on the Walnut Creek side of the hills.
  • Lakewood. Lakewood is a residential neighborhood in Walnut Creek, built as a postwar subdivision on the valley floor.
  • Northgate. Northgate runs up toward the Mount Diablo foothills on the eastern side of Walnut Creek.
  • Parkmead. Parkmead is a residential neighborhood on the southern side of Walnut Creek, near the creek the city is named for.
  • Rancho San Miguel. Rancho San Miguel is a residential subdivision in Walnut Creek that carries a rancho name.
  • Rossmoor. Rossmoor is a 55 and over community and it was a cattle ranch first.
  • Rudgear Estates. Rudgear Estates is a residential subdivision on the southern edge of Walnut Creek, off Rudgear Road.
  • Saranap. Saranap is not in Walnut Creek.
  • Tice Valley. Tice Valley is where Rossmoor came from.
  • Walnut Heights. Walnut Heights sits on the rising ground on the south side of Walnut Creek.
  • Woodlands. The Woodlands is a subdivision in the hills on the Walnut Creek side of the Lamorinda line.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $9,361, $112,338 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. Contra Costa County's 2026 one-unit loan limit sits at $1,249,125. That is the cap for conforming conventional and for FHA alike.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $990,472 here, transfer tax runs about $1,090 at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Custom is to split it, so about $545 a side, and who pays is set by the contract.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $11,886.

What waiting costs

On the same trailing rate, two years of waiting adds up to roughly $29,864 in price and payment combined, and five years to $91,901.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

item.content:encoded:
Pleasant Hill incorporated in 1961 to stop Concord from annexing it.

Pleasant Hill became a city to stop a neighbour. Concord was expanding west, and the voters here approved incorporation on November 7, 1961, with one city history giving November 14 and the sources differing by a week. That 1961 vote blocked Concord's westward expansion, and it is part of why Clayton on the far side kept pushing for its own city after a 1963 Concord annexation move. Diablo Valley College is here. The town had a post office from 1948, thirteen years before it had a city hall, and at least one account mistakes that post office year for the incorporation date.

Pleasant Hill has 13,939 housing units and 9.6 percent of them predate 1950. 60.0 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 62.6 percent, and the ACS median value is 1,077,100 dollars. ZHVI is about 973,000 dollars, up 1.3 percent over the year.

So this is largely a postwar city with a built downtown and a planned transit district on its southern edge, and those are three different markets.

On the tracts, pull the year built and the permit history, and ask about the panel, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof and the foundation bolting. On the hill neighborhoods, soils, drainage, retaining structures and a written fire insurance quote on the exact address.

Around the BART station, note that the transit village itself is unincorporated county ground at Contra Costa Centre, so confirm which jurisdiction the parcel is in before anything else. Then get the association budget and the reserve study, and walk to the station and time it.

And near Diablo Valley College, look at the block on a weekday in term and ask the city about parking restrictions.

And one habit worth keeping in this county. Pull the year built before you form any opinion on a listing, because it decides the entire inspection list and it is the single most useful number on a property profile. Then get the tax bill for the exact address off the county roll, not the listing estimate, and read which districts and assessments are on it. Those two documents cost nothing, they take a day, and between them they settle most of what a buyer actually needs to know before writing an offer.

What the market is doing right now

The value index puts a typical Pleasant Hill home at $973,036 on 2026-09-30, up 0.38 percent month over month and up 1.3 percent year over year.

Listing activity in Pleasant Hill for 2026-09. Active inventory is 57, up 7.5 percent from the prior month and up 0.9 percent from a year earlier. 36 new listings came on, down 10.0 percent month over month, and 32 went pending. Median days on market is 27, down 8.6 percent month over month and down 39.8 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $912,000 at $584 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,509 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $3,043.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $973,036, up 0.38 percent month over month, up 1.3 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $9,211, or $110,537 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 8 areas of Pleasant Hill. What each one actually is:

  • College Park. College Park is the Pleasant Hill neighborhood next to Diablo Valley College.
  • Downtown. Downtown Pleasant Hill is a built downtown, laid out long after the city's housing.
  • Gregory Gardens. Gregory Gardens is one of the postwar tracts on the northern side of Pleasant Hill.
  • Hidden Lakes. Hidden Lakes is a Pleasant Hill neighborhood on the rising ground, around the lakes it is named for.
  • Pleasant Hill Bart Area. The Pleasant Hill BART area is the transit district on the city's southern edge, and it is a different market from the tracts around it.
  • Poets Corner. Poets Corner is a Pleasant Hill neighborhood where the streets carry poets' names.
  • Shannon Hills. Shannon Hills is hill ground in Pleasant Hill.
  • Sherman Acres. Sherman Acres is a postwar residential neighborhood in Pleasant Hill.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $9,211 a month to own the typical home in Pleasant Hill, $110,537 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. For 2026, one-unit financing in Contra Costa County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $973,036 here, transfer tax runs about $1,070 at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Local practice splits it down the middle, roughly $535 each, though the contract decides.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $11,676.

What waiting costs

Waiting two years at this place's own trailing rate costs about $28,927, counting the price increase and the payment increase together. Over five years it is $88,993.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

Martinez has been the county seat since 1850, and it could not legally become a city for another 26 years.

Martinez was laid out in 1849 by Col. William M. Smith and named for Ygnacio Martinez. It became the county seat in 1850 and it has been ever since. It could not incorporate at the time, because it did not have the 200 registered voters the law required, and it did not become a city until 1876. Rumours that the oil companies were coming set off a real estate rush in 1912, and Shell located here in 1915. Alhambra Valley, on the western side of town, was inside the 1824 Rancho El Pinole grant to Ygnacio Martinez.

The John Muir National Historic Site is here. The house was built in 1883 by Dr. John Strentzel, Muir's father in law. Muir came to Martinez in 1880, lived in this house from 1890, and died in it in 1914. The city also claims the martini, from a local bartender's Martinez Special in 1849, though San Francisco and other cities claim it too and the claim is genuinely disputed. Joe DiMaggio was born here.

Martinez has 15,178 housing units and 14.0 percent of them predate 1950, a high pre war share for this county, behind El Cerrito, Richmond and San Pablo. 63.7 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 70.8 percent, the highest of the six, and the ACS median value is 859,800 dollars. Citywide ZHVI is about 750,000 dollars, down 1.3 percent over the year.

So this city runs two ways. The waterfront downtown and the older streets around it are pre war, with the long inspection list and the zoning question that come with a county seat downtown. The hill subdivisions and the eastern side are postwar tract housing, where the year built and the tract map tell you more than the neighborhood name does. Out in Alhambra Valley you add septic, well and the city limit line.

Pull the year built. It tells you which Martinez you are in.

Inside it

This report covers 6 areas of Martinez. What each one actually is:

  • Alhambra Valley. Alhambra Valley is the oldest named ground in Martinez.
  • Downtown Martinez. Downtown Martinez is a county seat downtown, and it has been the county seat since 1850.
  • Franklin Hills. Franklin Hills is hill ground on the Martinez side of the ridge.
  • Morello. Morello is a residential neighborhood in Martinez, along Morello Avenue on the city's eastern side.
  • Mountain View. Mountain View is a residential neighborhood in Martinez.
  • Virginia Hills. Virginia Hills sits on the rising ground in Martinez.

What it costs to own here

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $7,290 monthly, or $87,474 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

The 30-year fixed average is 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent in the same week last year. In Contra Costa County the 2026 one-unit limit is $1,249,125. It serves as the conforming conventional ceiling and the FHA ceiling at once.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

At 1.10 dollars per thousand, a $749,729 sale in Martinez carries about $825 in transfer tax. Convention puts about $412 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $8,997.

item.content:encoded:
Danville lost four incorporation votes before it won one.

Danville took four defeats to become a town. Valley wide incorporation went to a vote in 1964, 1967, 1973 and 1976 and failed every time. A home rule campaign started in 1980 and the voters approved it on June 8, 1982.

Eugene O'Neill won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1936 and spent the money building a house above Danville. Tao House is a Monterey Colonial by the architect Frederick Confer, and O'Neill and his wife lived in it from 1937 to 1944. In 1965 three local women, among them Darlene Blair and Lois Sizoo, formed an association to save it, and the place became a National Historic Landmark in 1971, a National Historic Site in 1976, and a National Park Service property in 1980. Getting in is unusual: the site is reached through a private gated road owned by neighbouring residents and visitors cannot drive their own cars to it.

Danville has 16,004 housing units and 1.8 percent of them predate 1950. 77.4 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 85.5 percent. The ACS median value is 1,681,700 dollars and ZHVI is about 1,821,000, up 0.2 percent over the year.

Only 1.8 percent of this housing stock predates 1950, so almost everything here is postwar or newer, on a detached lot, owner occupied. 85.5 percent owner occupancy is among the highest of any town in the county.

So the questions are postwar and newer questions. Pull the year built and the permit history. On anything recent, the association reserve study and the assessment districts, with the expiry year in writing. On the hill and eastern addresses toward Tassajara and Mount Diablo, soils, drainage, retaining walls, septic and well where they apply, and a written fire insurance quote on the exact address.

Out toward Tassajara, confirm whether the parcel is inside the town or in unincorporated county territory.

item.content:encoded:
San Ramon has the newest housing stock of any city in Contra Costa County. 0.4 percent of it predates 1950.

San Ramon incorporated in 1983, and it got there second. Danville lobbied the Local Agency Formation Commission first and succeeded in 1982, and San Ramon followed. The boundary fights before that are worth knowing: the 1967 incorporation proposal covered Alamo, Danville and south San Ramon joined by an 1,800 foot wide cherry stem drawn specifically to leave Bishop Ranch out. In 1978, 585 acres there became the Bishop Ranch business park, and it is the employment base this city was built around.

San Ramon has 30,744 housing units and 0.4 percent of them predate 1950, the newest housing stock of any city in this county. 63.5 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 70.9 percent. The ACS median value is 1,509,500 dollars. ZHVI is about 1,447,000 dollars, down 3.0 percent over the year, and that decline is the only one among the Lamorinda and San Ramon Valley markets.

That 3.0 percent decline is worth sitting with, because it is the only one in this group. Lafayette, Orinda, Moraga, Danville, Alamo and Diablo all rose over the same year. A market built this recently and this fast moves differently from its older neighbours.

So the buying questions are new construction questions. Get the association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure. Ask which community facilities districts the parcel sits in, what each levies and the year each expires, in writing from the county, because in Dougherty Valley that line runs for decades and does not come off with the mortgage. Ask the inspector about grading and drainage, since a young subdivision on engineered fill shows its settlement early.

And confirm the school assignment with the district. Boundaries in a development built this fast have been redrawn.

$1,447,415 is the typical San Ramon home as of 2026-09-30. Month over month that is up 0.01 percent, and over the year down 3.0 percent.

  • Monthly cost of owning it: $13,294, or $159,530 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 9 areas of San Ramon. What each one actually is:

  • Canyon Lakes. Canyon Lakes is a San Ramon community built around a golf course.
  • Country Club. The Country Club neighborhood sits on the eastern side of San Ramon near the golf course.
  • Dougherty Valley. Dougherty Valley is the large planned development on the eastern side of San Ramon, and it is the reason this city's housing stock is the newest in the county.
  • Downtown San Ramon. Downtown San Ramon is newer than the city, and the city is newer than most of its neighbours.
  • Gale Ranch. Gale Ranch is another of the Dougherty Valley villages, built out over the same period.
  • Henry Ranch. Henry Ranch is a smaller San Ramon subdivision on the higher ground.
  • Twin Creeks. Twin Creeks is one of the older residential neighborhoods in San Ramon, from before incorporation.
  • Westside San Ramon. Westside San Ramon is the older western side of the city, nearer the Bishop Ranch employment base.
  • Windemere. Windemere is one of the Dougherty Valley villages on San Ramon's eastern side.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical San Ramon home and the monthly carry lands near $13,294. That is $159,530 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $1,447,415 here, transfer tax runs about $1,592 at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Custom is to split it, so about $796 a side, and who pays is set by the contract.

item.content:encoded:
Antioch was a river landing, then a coal town, then the fastest growing housing market in the county.

Antioch started as a river landing. John Marsh, who owned Rancho Los Meganos, built a landing on the San Joaquin in 1848. The Smith twins founded a town just west of it in 1849 and called it Smith's Landing. The place also went by Marsh's Landing and East Antioch before it took the name of the biblical city. The year of that rename is not settled in the sources, so treat any single date for it with suspicion.

Then coal. It was found in 1859 near Horse Haven and the Black Diamond Mine opened in 1860. The boom founded four towns in these hills, Nortonville, Somersville, Stewartville and Black Diamond, and that last one is now the city of Pittsburg. Nortonville was the biggest and the oldest, with a peak population of about 1,000. Sand mining carried on after the coal and ended by the late 1940s, beaten by Belgian glass sand and the closing of the steel foundry. The ground is now Black Diamond Mines Regional Preserve, 6,000 acres under the East Bay Regional Park District.

Antioch has 38,629 housing units and 7.4 percent of them predate 1950. 78.3 percent are single family detached, second only to Brentwood among this county's larger cities. Owner occupancy runs 63.6 percent and the ACS median value is 629,700 dollars. Citywide ZHVI is about 590,000 dollars, down 0.7 percent over the year.

That 78.3 percent detached share is second only to Brentwood among this county's larger cities, and the 7.4 percent pre war share is near the bottom. Almost everything in Antioch is a detached house built after 1950, and a large part of it was built after 1990.

So the questions split by era. On the older stock in Rivertown, the pre war inspection list and the downtown zoning question. On the postwar tracts, the year built, the permit history and the panel. On the newer subdivisions along the southern edge, the association reserve study and the assessment districts, because Mello Roos out here runs into thousands a year and does not come off with the mortgage.

Ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and when each is scheduled to expire, in writing. Then drive Lone Tree Way and the Highway 4 corridor at your real commute hour.

What the market is doing right now

As of 2026-09-30 the typical Antioch home is worth $590,401. That is up 0.31 percent on the month and down 0.7 percent on the year.

Listing activity in Antioch for 2026-09. Active inventory is 185, up 2.2 percent from the prior month and down 7.5 percent from a year earlier. 78 new listings came on, down 11.4 percent month over month, and 90 went pending. Median days on market is 44, up 14.1 percent month over month and down 9.6 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $616,550 at $314 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,894 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,901.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $590,401, up 0.31 percent month over month, down 0.7 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $5,918, or $71,019 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 10 areas of Antioch. What each one actually is:

  • Black Diamond. Black Diamond is named for the coal.
  • Country Hills. Country Hills is a residential subdivision in the Antioch hills.
  • Deer Valley. Deer Valley is on the southern edge of Antioch, out where the city meets open ground.
  • Hillcrest. Hillcrest is the Antioch neighborhood around Hillcrest Avenue, on the city's eastern side.
  • Lone Tree. Lone Tree is the Antioch neighborhood along Lone Tree Way, one of the main east west routes across the city.
  • Mira Vista Hills. Mira Vista Hills is hill ground in Antioch, south of the old river town.
  • Prewett Ranch. Prewett Ranch is a newer Antioch subdivision on the city's southern side.
  • Rivertown. Rivertown is the original Antioch, down on the San Joaquin River where the landing was.
  • Sunset. Sunset is a residential neighborhood in Antioch.
  • The Vineyards. The Vineyards is one of Antioch's newer subdivisions, on the southern edge of the city.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $5,918, $71,019 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. The conforming and FHA ceiling for a one-unit property in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125 in 2026.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

At 1.10 dollars per thousand, a $590,401 sale in Antioch carries about $649 in transfer tax. Convention puts about $325 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $7,085.

What waiting costs

Price and payment together, a two year wait here runs about -$9,592. Stretch it to five and the figure is -$28,647.

This rests on one observed year carried forward. The two year figure is the defensible one; the five year figure is arithmetic, not a forecast.

item.content:encoded:
Pittsburg has had three names and a steel mill through all of them.

Pittsburg has had three names. Col. Jonathan D. Stevenson, a New Yorker, bought the Rancho Los Medanos grant in 1849 and founded a town he called New York of the Pacific. It had failed by 1850. Coal out of Nortonville turned the waterfront into a shipping port, and the landing took the name Black Diamond from the mining firm. The town incorporated in 1903 under that name, though some accounts have the post office using Black Diamond as far back as 1868.

Steel made the third name. C.A. Hooper bought the land in 1900 and helped bring in Columbia Steel. The plant opened here in 1910 with one foundry and 60 employees and poured its first heat that November. One source puts the opening at 1906. Columbia Steel became a US Steel subsidiary in 1930 and the mill runs today as USS POSCO. On February 11, 1911 the citizens voted to rename the town Pittsburg, for Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and dropped the h. Camp Stoneman here was a major Army staging area through World War II and Korea.

Pittsburg has 24,482 housing units and 8.3 percent of them predate 1950. 68.2 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 62.3 percent, and the ACS median value is 597,900 dollars. Citywide ZHVI is about 559,000 dollars, down 0.8 percent over the year.

So a buyer here is mostly buying postwar housing in a city with a working industrial waterfront. The split runs north to south. Old Town and the streets near the water are the oldest, with the pre war inspection list and a zoning question, because the permitted use on the next parcel over can be industrial. The subdivisions climbing south toward Kirker Pass are postwar and newer, and out there the tract map, the assessment districts and the commute over the pass are what matter.

Ask for the site history in writing on anything near the water. Pull the year built and the permit history everywhere. And drive Kirker Pass Road at your real commute hour before you decide.

  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

  • Highlands Ranch. Highlands Ranch is a residential subdivision in the Pittsburg hills.
  • Kirker Pass Area. The Kirker Pass area is the southern end of Pittsburg, where the road climbs over the hills toward Concord.
  • Los Medanos. Los Medanos is the name on the original land grant.
  • Old Town Pittsburg. Old Town Pittsburg is the waterfront, and the waterfront is why the city exists.
  • San Marco. San Marco is one of Pittsburg's newer subdivisions, on the higher ground south of the old town.
  • Vista Del Mar. Vista Del Mar is a residential neighborhood in Pittsburg.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $5,647 a month to own the typical home in Pittsburg, $67,767 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. For 2026, one-unit financing in Contra Costa County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

On a home at $558,908 here, transfer tax runs about $615 at 1.10 dollars per thousand. It is normally split down the middle, about $307 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $6,707.

item.content:encoded:
Oakley planned its downtown three years before it became a city.

Oakley is the newest city in Contra Costa County. It incorporated on July 1, 1999 and has been reported as the eleventh newest city in the state. The ground was part of Rancho Los Meganos, granted in 1835, and the townsite was settled around 1897 with a post office in 1898. The city planned its downtown before it existed as a city: the work began in the early 1990s while this was still unincorporated, and the county adopted the Old Town Oakley Specific Plan in 1996. It is a general law city with a council manager government and a five member council elected by district, on the San Joaquin River Delta.

Oakley has 13,944 housing units and 3.0 percent of them predate 1950. 90.6 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 78.8 percent, and the ACS median value is 660,200 dollars. ZHVI is about 654,000 dollars, down 0.5 percent over the year.

90.6 percent detached across 13,944 units, with 3.0 percent of the stock pre war. This is a Delta farm town that became a suburb fast, and the city is younger than most of its housing.

So the assessment question comes first. Ask which community facilities districts the parcel sits in, what each levies and the year each expires, in writing from the county. Then the association budget and the reserve study where there is an association, not the dues figure.

Ask the inspector about grading and drainage, since a young subdivision on engineered fill shows settlement in its first fifteen years. In Old Town, read the Old Town Oakley Specific Plan the county adopted in 1996, because it is public and it says what is intended on those streets.

And drive Laurel Road and the Highway 4 corridor at your real commute hour.

And one habit worth keeping in this county. Pull the year built before you form any opinion on a listing, because it decides the entire inspection list and it is the single most useful number on a property profile. Then get the tax bill for the exact address off the county roll, not the listing estimate, and read which districts and assessments are on it. Those two documents cost nothing, they take a day, and between them they settle most of what a buyer actually needs to know before writing an offer.

The man who built it left a museum behind. Kenneth Behring developed Blackhawk, and a partnership he began with Don Williams in 1982 opened the Blackhawk Automotive Museum in August 1988, called the Behring Auto Museum in some accounts. It started as a home for his car collection and now runs four more galleries alongside it: The Spirit of the Old West, Art of Africa, Into China and World of Nature. It is a subsidiary of the non profit Behring Global Educational Foundation and an affiliate of the Smithsonian Institution. It sits inside Blackhawk Plaza and is not affiliated with the shopping centre. Behring also owned the Seattle Seahawks and founded the Wheelchair Foundation. He died in 2019 at 91.

item.content:encoded:
Discovery Bay is a Delta community with navigable water running into the neighborhoods, and 90.1 percent of it is owner occupied.

Discovery Bay is unincorporated Contra Costa County territory out on the San Joaquin River Delta east of Brentwood, built as a planned waterfront community. Brentwood nearby takes its name from John Marsh's ancestral home in Essex, England, was bought up by the British investment house Balfour, Guthrie and Co. in 1910, and incorporated on January 21, 1948. Oakley to the north became the county's newest city on July 1, 1999. Discovery Bay stayed county ground.

Discovery Bay has 6,053 housing units and 2.8 percent of them predate 1950. 90.8 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 90.1 percent, among the highest in the county. The ACS median value is 832,000 dollars and ZHVI is about 775,000 dollars, down 0.9 percent over the year.

So the water is most of the purchase and it carries the questions. Get the flood zone determination for the parcel with a written insurance quote, and ask the inspector about settlement and about the condition and ownership of any bulkhead, levee or revetment the property sits behind. On the water that is the most expensive thing that can go wrong and it is frequently shared. Ask who owns and who maintains the channel and the dock, get the dock permit and its condition in writing, and ask whether dredging is an association obligation and when it was last done.

A Delta levee is an insurance question too, so get the flood determination with a written quote before your contingencies expire. Then confirm the parcel is unincorporated and get the association budget and the reserve study.

One thing worth spelling out, because it catches buyers. In an unincorporated place there is no city hall standing between you and the county. Your building permits and inspections come from the county, code enforcement is the county's, the Sheriff answers calls unless a special district provides policing, and fire, water and sewer frequently come from separate districts that each levy on the parcel. So get the full list of districts for the address off the county's tax roll, not the listing, and read what each one charges. Then ask the county's Local Agency Formation Commission whether the parcel sits in any city's sphere of influence, because that is where future annexation would start and it is a public record.

And one habit worth keeping in this county. Pull the year built before you form any opinion on a listing, because it decides the entire inspection list and it is the single most useful number on a property profile. Then get the tax bill for the exact address off the county roll, not the listing estimate, and read which districts and assessments are on it. Those two documents cost nothing, they take a day, and between them they settle most of what a buyer actually needs to know before writing an offer.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. For 2026, one-unit financing in Contra Costa County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

Discovery Bay charges 1.10 per thousand, so the typical $775,031 home owes roughly $853 at transfer. Convention puts about $426 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.
