item.title: Kensington: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Kensington housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,490,293, up 0.90 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Kensington has never been a city. 96.4 percent of it is detached houses and 59.7 percent of them were built before 1950.

Kensington is unincorporated Contra Costa County territory on the hill above Berkeley and El Cerrito. El Cerrito below it incorporated as a village on August 23, 1917 on a vote of 158 to 131, after people leaving San Francisco following the 1906 earthquake settled this slope on what was then Don Victor Castro's Rancho San Pablo. Kensington stayed county ground and remains so.

Kensington has 2,207 housing units. 59.7 percent predate 1950 and 96.4 percent are single family detached, among the highest shares of any place in the county. Owner occupancy runs 86.8 percent and the ACS median value is 1,539,000 dollars. ZHVI is about 1,490,000 dollars, up 5.3 percent over the year, among the stronger moves in the county.

So two lists cover almost every address here, and both are long. The pre war list: foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, the condition of original windows and siding, the permit history. And the hill list: soils, drainage, where water leaves the parcel in a wet month, the condition and ownership of every retaining structure, and a written fire insurance quote on the exact address with the risk rating explained.

Then confirm the parcel is unincorporated and ask which school district serves it.

In an unincorporated place the service districts are the government, and Kensington's are unusually well documented. The Kensington Police Protection and Community Services District was formed in 1946, first as the Kensington Police Protection District, and reorganised under the community services district law in 1953. Accounts of its renaming differ, a community timeline giving 1993 and the county's LAFCO giving 1995. Fire ran separately for most of that time: the Kensington Fire Protection District was formed in 1937 and in 1995 it contracted with the City of El Cerrito for fire and emergency service. Effective October 1, 2025 the fire district consolidated into the community services district.

So ask who answers a call at this address and under which district, and ask what each district levies on the parcel. In a place with no city, those are the questions a city would otherwise answer for you.

One thing worth spelling out, because it catches buyers. In an unincorporated place there is no city hall standing between you and the county. Your building permits and inspections come from the county, code enforcement is the county's, the Sheriff answers calls unless a special district provides policing, and fire, water and sewer frequently come from separate districts that each levy on the parcel. So get the full list of districts for the address off the county's tax roll, not the listing, and read what each one charges. Then ask the county's Local Agency Formation Commission whether the parcel sits in any city's sphere of influence, because that is where future annexation would start and it is a public record.

And one habit worth keeping in this county. Pull the year built before you form any opinion on a listing, because it decides the entire inspection list and it is the single most useful number on a property profile. Then get the tax bill for the exact address off the county roll, not the listing estimate, and read which districts and assessments are on it. Those two documents cost nothing, they take a day, and between them they settle most of what a buyer actually needs to know before writing an offer.

What the market is doing right now

As of 2026-09-30 the typical Kensington home is worth $1,490,293. That is up 0.90 percent on the month and up 5.3 percent on the year.

Realtor.com does not publish monthly listing metrics for Kensington, so there is no inventory, days on market or asking price figure to report here. The value series above is measured separately and is unaffected.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,490,293, up 0.90 percent month over month, up 5.3 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $13,663, or $163,958 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 1 area of Kensington. What each one actually is:

  • Kensington. Kensington is unincorporated, 96.4 percent detached, and 59.7 percent of it was built before 1950.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $13,663, $163,958 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. In Contra Costa County the 2026 one-unit limit is $1,249,125. It serves as the conforming conventional ceiling and the FHA ceiling at once.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Kensington charges 1.10 per thousand, so the typical $1,490,293 home owes roughly $1,639 at transfer. Convention puts about $820 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against Richmond at 13.50. Same county, same price, and the spread is $18,480.

What waiting costs

Price and payment together, a two year wait here runs about $188,280. Stretch it to five and the figure is $615,507.

Treat it as a scenario, not a prediction. The appreciation input is one year of observed change carried forward, and five years of compounding on one year of data flatters the result.

The full report

For the tables, the financing detail, the tax math, the holding costs, the buyer programs, the ADU rules and the sources, the full Kensington report has all of it. It is rebuilt every month when the new data publishes. Read it at https://myrealtoraye.github.io/neighborhood-reports/kensington/.

item.title: Stockton: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Stockton housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $422,451, up 0.10 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Stockton exists because a man gave up on gold. Captain Charles Maria Weber, who came from Germany, acquired Rancho Campo de los Franceses and founded the town in 1849. He tried mining first and worked out that selling supplies to the people going to the mines paid better. The site sat at the head of navigation on the San Joaquin River, so the goods came by water and the miners came to him. He laid the place out as Tuleburg and then settled on Stockton, for Commodore Robert F. Stockton. The city incorporated on July 23, 1850 and took its charter from the state in 1851.

The other thing every buyer here should know is the bankruptcy, because it is finished and the facts are public. Stockton filed Chapter 9 on July 28, 2012 against more than 2 billion dollars in labour agreements and long term debt, the largest bankrupt city in the country until Detroit filed the next year. A judge found it eligible on April 1, 2013. Chief Bankruptcy Judge Christopher Klein confirmed the plan of adjustment on October 30, 2014 and signed the confirmation order on February 4, 2015, and the city exited effective February 25, 2015. Every major creditor settled except Franklin Templeton Investments. The payment schedule under that plan runs to 2053.

Stockton has 105,162 housing units and 13.8 percent of them predate 1950. 66.8 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 53.9 percent, and the ACS median value is 440,900 dollars. ZHVI is about 422,000 dollars, down 1.7 percent over the year, the lowest level of any city in the three counties covered here.

So ask what the plan means for the address. The 2053 payment schedule is a public document and it shapes what this city can spend on streets, parks and emergency services for the next three decades. A buyer is entitled to read it before committing.

So the market splits by era and by ground. 13.8 percent of this housing stock is pre war, and around the Miracle Mile, the Magnolia Historic District, downtown and the older east side that is the inspection list you are facing. The north side and the waterway communities are postwar and newer, where the association reserve study and the question of who maintains the lake or the channel are the purchase. South of the river at Weston Ranch, the levee is the purchase.

Pull the year built. Get the tax bill for the exact address off the county roll, not the listing estimate. In the historic district, read the district rules before you plan any exterior change. And on anything near the port or the airport, ask for the site history in writing and get the noise contour map.

What the market is doing right now

Typical home value in Stockton is $422,451 as of 2026-09-30, up 0.10 percent from the month before and down 1.7 percent over the year.

Listing activity in Stockton for 2026-09. Active inventory is 557, up 5.9 percent from the prior month and down 13.5 percent from a year earlier. 218 new listings came on, down 10.7 percent month over month, and 251 went pending. Median days on market is 59, up 6.6 percent month over month and up 2.7 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $423,750 at $279 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,524 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,091.

  • Typical home value: $422,451, up 0.10 percent month over month, down 1.7 percent over the year.

  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.

  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.27 percent (Stockton effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 22 areas of Stockton. What each one actually is:

  • Airport District. The Airport District is south of downtown Stockton, around the airport.
  • August. August is an older neighborhood on Stockton's east side.
  • Banner Island. Banner Island is on the downtown Stockton waterfront.
  • Bear Creek. Bear Creek runs through north Stockton and the neighborhood takes its name.
  • Boggs Tract. Boggs Tract sits against Stockton's working industrial waterfront.
  • Brookside Estates. Brookside Estates is part of the Brookside development in north Stockton.
  • Brookside. Brookside is a north Stockton community built around waterways and a golf course.
  • Cabral. Cabral is a Stockton residential neighborhood.
  • Civic Center. The Civic Center area is Stockton's government district.
  • Conway Homes. Conway Homes is a Stockton neighborhood on the city's south side.
  • Country Club. The Country Club neighborhood is on Stockton's north side.
  • Downtown. Downtown Stockton is where Weber laid the town out in 1849, at the head of navigation on the San Joaquin River.
  • El Dorado. El Dorado is a Stockton neighborhood named for the gold country the city supplied.
  • Fremont. Fremont is an older Stockton neighborhood.
  • French Camp Corridor. The French Camp corridor runs south out of Stockton toward French Camp, and parts of it are unincorporated county ground.
  • Garden Acres. Garden Acres is on Stockton's eastern side and part of this area is unincorporated county ground.
  • Kentfield. Kentfield is a Stockton residential neighborhood.
  • Lincoln Village West. Lincoln Village West sits on the water on Stockton's north side.
  • Lincoln Village. Lincoln Village is a north Stockton neighborhood, and part of this area is unincorporated county ground.
  • Lincoln. Lincoln is a Stockton neighborhood on the city's north side.
  • Magnolia Historic District. The Magnolia Historic District is a designated district, and the designation is the first thing to understand about buying in it.
  • Miracle Mile. The Miracle Mile is Stockton's old commercial strip and the housing around it is some of the city's oldest.

What it costs to own here

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $4,459 monthly, or $53,505 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. The conforming and FHA ceiling for a one-unit property in San Joaquin County is $832,750 in 2026.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical Stockton home, $422,451, comes to roughly $465 at a rate of 1.10 per thousand. Local practice splits it down the middle, roughly $232 each, though the contract decides.

What waiting costs

Waiting two years at this place's own trailing rate costs about -$16,396, counting the price increase and the payment increase together. Over five years it is -$48,252.

One year of data, extended. That is worth saying plainly, because compounding it out to five years makes the total look more certain than it is.

item.content:encoded:
Lodi started as a railroad stop called Mokelumne Station, when the Central Pacific put a station here in 1869. The renaming is a genuine muddle. A city page says the Legislature changed the name in 1874, to stop the confusion with Mokelumne City and Mokelumne Hill. Britannica gives 1873 and suggests a racehorse of the day. A city records finding aid says the residents did it themselves in 1878. Another account credits Assembly Bill 639 and points at Lodi, Italy. Residents voted on incorporation in 1906 and the county Board of Supervisors declared Lodi incorporated on December 6 of that year.

The arch is the landmark. E. B. Brown built it in 1907 for the first Lodi Tokay Carnival, an event that exists today as the Lodi Grape Festival, and a city page calls it the oldest standing welcome arch in the United States. It was restored in 1956 after it had deteriorated into a hazard. The carnival was built around the Flame Tokay, a grape developed here, and the whole point of it in 1907 was to advertise that grape.

Lodi has 24,806 housing units and 15.9 percent of them predate 1950, the highest pre war share of any city in San Joaquin County. 64.9 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 56.8 percent, and the ACS median value is 492,500 dollars. ZHVI is about 509,000 dollars, down 1.4 percent over the year.

That 15.9 percent pre war share is the highest in the county, so in Lodi the inspection list is a pre war list more often than anywhere else in San Joaquin.

One research warning specific to this town. The visitor bureau, the chamber and the local paper will all confirm an address, and their published hours routinely disagree with each other. Use them for days and confirm hours with the business.

And get the tax bill for the exact address off the county roll, not the listing estimate.

Tracy is a railroad town and the date is exact. It was founded on September 8, 1878 and named for Lathrop J. Tracy, a grain merchant and railroad director from Mansfield, Ohio, who as far as the record shows never lived here. The town came out of a junction: Southern Pacific built its line around Suisun Bay in September 1878 and made the connection three miles east of Ellis, with one account calling it a Central Pacific junction. The railroad shut the Ellis coaling station and moved its employees and their families to Lathrop and to the new Tracy station. Southern Pacific moved its operational headquarters from Lathrop to Tracy in 1894. Tracy became a city in 1910.

Tracy has 30,228 housing units and 7.1 percent of them predate 1950. 81.0 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 65.0 percent, and the ACS median value is 699,000 dollars. That 4.1 percent decline deserves its own paragraph, because it is the steepest of any city in San Joaquin County over the same twelve months and among the steepest in the three counties covered here. Tracy is a commuter market at the far edge of the Bay Area's reach, and markets like that move further in both directions than the places they feed.

It became the state's 483rd city on July 1, 2024, after voters approved Measures D and E on March 5 of that year, and before that it was a community services district. The place was planned long before it was a city: San Joaquin County adopted the Mountain House Master Plan as a General Plan amendment in 1993, the Board of Supervisors approved the planned community in 1994, and construction started in 2001. The Yokuts were the original inhabitants of this ground. It is the best available measure and it is not a Mountain House city index, so read it as the ZIP figure it is and work from closed comparable sales on the specific streets.

A municipality incorporated in 2024 is still building out its own services, its own revenue base and its own general plan, so ask the city directly what it now provides and what the county or a district still provides, and ask what the community services district's obligations became on incorporation. Those answers determine your tax bill and your services and they are changing.

The town is laid out as named villages, each planned as a unit, so pull the village plan and the tract map from the county and read what was actually approved for the streets around the address.

Joshua Cowell arrived in 1861 and the place carried his name, but when the Central Pacific came through in 1873 a new one was needed, because a Cowell's Station already existed to the south near Tracy. They settled on Monteca and the first railroad tickets came back printed Manteca. The Manteca Bulletin treats the ticket misprint as the account with the most credence; a weaker telling puts the error in a newspaper. The town incorporated in 1918, with May 28 given as the date, and Cowell became its first mayor.

The rail line that named this town shaped the whole southern end of the county. The Central Pacific came through here in 1873 and the farm towns along it, Ripon and Escalon among them, sit where they do because of it. Ripon was called Stanislaus Station before it was Ripon. item.title: Lathrop: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Lathrop housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $620,627, down 0.39 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Lathrop began as a depot called Wilson's Station in 1868, and it grew up as a railroad town that then lost its headquarters to a neighbour. The city itself is young: it incorporated in 1989 and adopted its first General Plan in 1991. Southern Pacific moved its operational headquarters from Lathrop to Tracy in 1894, and when the railroad shut the Ellis coaling station in 1878 it had moved those employees and their families to Lathrop and to the new Tracy station. The town sits on the San Joaquin River and the river is the defining feature of buying here.

Lathrop has 9,092 housing units and 1.0 percent of them predate 1950, the newest housing stock of any city in San Joaquin County. 93.5 percent are single family detached, the highest detached share of any city in the county, owner occupancy runs 85.3 percent, and the ACS median value is 643,600 dollars. ZHVI is about 621,000 dollars, down 3.8 percent over the year.

That 1.0 percent pre war share is the lowest of any city in the county and the 93.5 percent detached share is the highest of any city in it. Lathrop is new detached housing on river ground, and the river is the subject.

So before anything else, ask the county and the reclamation district which levee protects the parcel, what its certification status is, and who maintains it. Then get the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote before your contingencies expire. Levee certification drives the insurance and what can be built, and in a city built out on the San Joaquin it is the first question, not the last.

Then ask which community facilities districts the parcel sits in, what each levies and the year each expires, in writing. Get the association budget and the reserve study. And ask the inspector about grading, drainage and settlement.

And get the tax bill for the exact address off the county roll, not the listing estimate, and read which districts and assessments appear on it. On river ground in a city this new, that one document and the levee answer together cover most of what a buyer needs before writing an offer.

What the market is doing right now

As of 2026-09-30 the typical Lathrop home is worth $620,627. That is down 0.39 percent on the month and down 3.8 percent on the year.

Listing activity in Lathrop for 2026-09. Active inventory is 127, down 0.8 percent from the prior month and up 14.9 percent from a year earlier. 36 new listings came on, down 10.0 percent month over month, and 54 went pending. Median days on market is 61, up 21.0 percent month over month and up 17.5 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $679,975 at $295 per square foot, on a median listing of 2,351 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $3,056.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $620,627, down 0.39 percent month over month, down 3.8 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $6,390, or $76,685 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, San Joaquin County: $832,750. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.72 percent (Lathrop effective rate).

Inside it

This report covers 5 areas of Lathrop. What each one actually is:

  • Historic Lathrop. Historic Lathrop is the old railroad town, and in a city where 1.0 percent of the housing predates 1950 this is where the age is.
  • Mossdale Landing. Mossdale Landing is on the San Joaquin River in Lathrop.
  • River Islands. River Islands is the large planned development on the river side of Lathrop, and the levees are the first subject.
  • Stonebridge. Stonebridge is a Lathrop residential subdivision.
  • Woodfield. Woodfield is a residential subdivision in Lathrop.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $6,390 a month to own the typical home in Lathrop, $76,685 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. In San Joaquin County the 2026 one-unit limit is $832,750. It serves as the conforming conventional ceiling and the FHA ceiling at once.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Figure $683 in transfer tax on a $620,627 sale here, at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Expect it split, near enough $341 apiece, with the contract having the final say.

What waiting costs

Price and payment together, a two year wait here runs about -$53,299. Stretch it to five and the figure is -$152,051.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.
